records.patched_text: "Have you ever thought of marrying off your wayward son Anatole?" she asked. "They say old maids have a passion for matchmaking, and though I don't feel that weakness in myself just yet, I do know a young woman who is very unhappy with her father. She's a relation of yours — Princess Mary Bolkonskaya."

Anna Pavlovna's drawing room was gradually filling up. The highest society of Petersburg was gathered there: people who differed widely in age and temperament but who all belonged to the same social world. Prince Vasili's daughter, the beautiful Helene, came to collect her father for the ambassador's party; she wore a ball gown and her badge as lady-in-waiting. The youthful little Princess Bolkonskaya, known as the most captivating woman in Petersburg, was also there. She had married the previous winter and, being pregnant, no longer attended large gatherings — only small receptions. Prince Vasili's son Hippolyte had arrived with Mortemart, whom he introduced. The Abbé Morio and many others had come as well.

[Speaking in French] "You know," said the princess in the same tone of voice, still in French, turning to a general, "my husband is abandoning me? He's going off to get himself killed. Tell me — what is this awful war even for?" she added, turning to Prince Vasili, and without waiting for an answer she turned to speak to his daughter, the beautiful Helene.

Anna Pavlovna's reception was in full swing. The spindles hummed steadily and ceaselessly on all sides. Aside from the aunt — beside whom sat only one elderly lady whose thin, careworn face seemed rather out of place in this brilliant company — the entire gathering had arranged itself into three groups. One, mostly male, had formed around the abbé. Another, made up of younger people, clustered around the beautiful Princess Helene, Prince Vasili's daughter, and the little Princess Bolkonskaya, who was very pretty and rosy-cheeked, though perhaps a bit plump for her age. The third group was gathered around Mortemart and Anna Pavlovna.
"Come here, Helene dear," said Anna Pavlovna to the beautiful young princess who was sitting some distance away, at the center of another group.

The princess smiled. She rose with the same unchanging smile she had worn since entering the room — the smile of a flawlessly beautiful woman. With a light rustle of her white dress trimmed with moss and ivy, with a gleam of white shoulders, glossy hair, and sparkling diamonds, she passed between the men who stepped aside for her. She looked at none of them, yet smiled at all of them, as though graciously granting each one the privilege of admiring her beautiful figure and shapely shoulders, back, and bosom — which, as was the fashion, were very much on display — and she seemed to bring the glamour of a ballroom with her as she crossed toward Anna Pavlovna. Helene was so stunning that she showed not the slightest trace of flirtation; on the contrary, she almost seemed embarrassed by her own overwhelming beauty. She appeared to wish, but to be unable, to lessen its effect.
The little princess had also left the tea table and followed Helene.

Just then another guest entered the drawing room: Prince Andrew Bolkonski, the little princess's husband. He was a very handsome young man of medium height, with firm, sharply defined features. Everything about him — from his weary, bored expression to his quiet, measured stride — stood in the sharpest contrast to his lively little wife. It was clear that he not only knew everyone in the room but found them all so tiresome that it exhausted him to look at or listen to them. And of all the faces he found so tedious, none seemed to bore him quite as much as his pretty wife's. He turned away from her with a grimace that marred his handsome face, kissed Anna Pavlovna's hand, and squinting slightly, surveyed the entire company.

Prince Andrew screwed up his eyes and looked away. Pierre, who had been watching him with glad, affectionate eyes from the moment he entered the room, now came up and took his arm. Before Prince Andrew could even look around, he frowned again — annoyed at whoever was touching his arm — but when he saw Pierre's beaming face, he broke into an unexpectedly warm and genuine smile.

"No, impossible!" said Prince Andrew, laughing and squeezing Pierre's hand to show that there was no need to ask. He wanted to say something more, but just then Prince Vasili and his daughter stood up to leave, and the two young men rose to let them pass.

His daughter, Princess Helene, passed between the chairs, lightly gathering up the folds of her gown, her smile shining even more brilliantly on her beautiful face. Pierre gazed at her with fascinated, almost frightened eyes as she swept past him.
"Very lovely," said Prince Andrew.
[Speaking in French] "Papa, we're going to be late," said Princess Helene, turning her beautiful head and glancing back over her sculpted shoulder as she waited by the door.
Prince Andrew looked Anna Pavlovna straight in the face with a sardonic smile.
"That's doubtful," said Prince Andrew. "The vicomte is quite right in saying that things have already gone too far. I think it will be very difficult to go back to the old order."
"Bonaparte himself has said so," remarked Prince Andrew with a sarcastic smile.

"'I showed them the path to glory, but they did not follow it,'" Prince Andrew continued after a brief silence, again quoting Napoleon's words. "'I opened my antechambers and they came crowding in.' I don't know how far he was justified in saying that."

Prince Andrew watched with an amused smile, looking from Pierre to the vicomte and from the vicomte to their hostess. In the first moment of Pierre's outburst, Anna Pavlovna had been horrified, despite all her social experience. But when she saw that Pierre's blasphemous words had not outraged the vicomte, and had satisfied herself that it was impossible to shut Pierre up, she rallied her forces and joined the vicomte in a vigorous counterattack on the young orator.

"How do you expect him to answer all of you at once?" said Prince Andrew. "Besides, when judging a statesman, you have to distinguish between his actions as a private individual, as a general, and as an emperor. At least that's how it seems to me."

"One must admit," Prince Andrew continued, "that Napoleon the man was great on the bridge at Arcola, and in the hospital at Jaffa where he clasped the hands of plague victims. But... there are other actions that are hard to justify."
Prince Andrew, who had clearly been trying to soften the awkwardness of Pierre's remarks, stood up and signaled to his wife that it was time to go.
"You give me your word of honor not to go?"
"Is the Englishman bragging? Hm? Are we ready?" said Anatole.

"Fine. Fifty imperials that I will drink an entire bottle of rum without taking it from my mouth, sitting out there on that ledge" — he leaned down and pointed to the sloping surface outside the window — "without holding on to anything. Agreed?"

"That's what modern education gets you," declared the visitor. "Apparently, while he was abroad, the young man was allowed to do whatever he pleased. Now in Petersburg, I hear he's been up to such terrible things that he was expelled by the police."

"He's exactly the same as ever," replied Anna Mikhaylovna, "overflowing with charm. His position hasn't gone to his head at all. He said to me, 'I'm sorry I can do so little for you, dear Princess. I'm at your disposal.' Yes, he's a fine man and a very kind relative. But, Nataly, you know how I love my son — I would do anything for his happiness! And my affairs are in such a bad state that my situation is truly desperate," Anna Mikhaylovna went on sadly, lowering her voice. "My wretched lawsuit eats up everything I have and gets nowhere. Would you believe it — I literally don't have a penny and have no idea how to outfit Boris for the army." She took out her handkerchief and began to cry. "I need five hundred rubles, and all I have is a single twenty-five-ruble note. I'm in such a state... My only hope now is Count Cyril Vladimirovich Bezukhov. If he won't help his own godson — you know he's Boris's godfather — and give him something for his upkeep, all my efforts will have been for nothing... I won't be able to equip him."

"I often think — though perhaps it's a sin," said the princess, "that here is Count Cyril Vladimirovich Bezukhov, so rich, all alone... that enormous fortune... and what is his life worth? It's a burden to him, while Boris's life is only just beginning..."

"Are you going to Count Cyril Vladimirovich, my dear?" asked the count, coming out of the dining room into the anteroom. "If he's feeling better, do ask Pierre to come to dinner. He's been to our house before, you know — he danced with the children. Be sure to invite him, my dear. We'll see how our cook Taras outdoes himself today. He claims Count Orlov never gave a dinner as fine as ours will be!"
"Prince, to err is human, * but..." replied the doctor, swallowing his r's and pronouncing the Latin words with a French accent.
* To err is human.

At Bald Hills, the estate of Prince Nicholas Andreevich Bolkonski, the arrival of young Prince Andrew and his wife was expected any day, but this didn't disrupt the old prince's rigid household routine. General-in-Chief Prince Nicholas Andreevich—nicknamed "the King of Prussia" in society—had been living at his country estate continuously since Emperor Paul had exiled him there, together with his daughter, Princess Mary, and her companion, Mademoiselle Bourienne. Though the new reign had made him free to return to the capitals, he continued to live in the country, remarking that anyone who wanted to see him could make the hundred-mile trip from Moscow to Bald Hills, while he himself needed nobody and nothing. He liked to say there are only two sources of human vice—idleness and superstition—and only two virtues—activity and intelligence. He personally oversaw his daughter's education, and to develop these two virtues in her, gave her lessons in algebra and geometry until she was twenty and organized her life so that every hour was accounted for. He himself was perpetually busy: writing his memoirs, solving problems in higher mathematics, turning snuffboxes on a lathe, working in the garden, or supervising the construction that was always underway on his estate. Since regularity is the first condition of productivity, regularity in his household was maintained to the highest degree of precision. He always came to meals not just at the same hour but at the same minute. With everyone around him, from his daughter down to the servants, the prince was sharp and unfailingly demanding—not out of cruelty, but with a severity that inspired the kind of fear and respect that few genuinely cruel men could have commanded. Although he was retired and no longer wielded political influence, every senior official appointed to the province felt duty-bound to pay him a visit, and they waited in his lofty antechamber—alongside the architect, the gardener, and Princess Mary—until the prince appeared at precisely the appointed time. Everyone in that waiting room experienced the same mix of respect and dread when the enormously tall study door swung open to reveal the small figure of the old man: powdered wig, small withered hands, and bushy gray eyebrows that, when he frowned, could hide the sharp gleam of his youthful, piercing eyes.

All Moscow talks of nothing but war. One of my two brothers is already abroad; the other is with the Guards, who are about to march for the frontier. Our dear Emperor has left Petersburg, and it's believed he intends to expose his precious person to the dangers of war. God grant that the Corsican monster who is destroying the peace of Europe may be overthrown by the angel whom the Almighty, in His goodness, has given us as our sovereign! To say nothing of my brothers, this war has robbed me of one of the bonds dearest to my heart. I mean young Nicholas Rostov, who was so passionately enthusiastic that he couldn't bear to remain idle and has left the university to join the army. I will confess to you, dear Mary, that despite his extreme youth, his departure for the army was a great sorrow for me. This young man, of whom I told you last summer, is so noble-spirited and full of that genuine youthfulness one so rarely finds anymore among our old men of twenty—and above all, he is so honest and has so much heart. He is so pure and poetic that my relationship with him, brief as it was, has been one of the sweetest comforts to my poor heart, which has already suffered so much. Someday I'll tell you about our parting and everything that was said. It's all still too fresh. Ah, dear friend, you're lucky not to know these sharp joys and sorrows. You are fortunate, because the sorrows are usually stronger! I know perfectly well that Count Nicholas is too young ever to be more than a friend to me, but this sweet friendship, this poetic, pure bond, was exactly what my heart needed. But enough of this! The main news, the talk of all Moscow, is the death of old Count Bezukhov and his inheritance. Can you imagine! The three princesses received almost nothing, Prince Vasili got nothing at all, and it's Monsieur Pierre who has inherited everything and has been officially recognized as legitimate—so he is now Count Bezukhov and the owner of the greatest fortune in Russia. People say Prince Vasili played a thoroughly contemptible role in the whole affair and went back to Petersburg completely humiliated.

Just then, a closed carriage and a hooded cart pulled up to the front porch. Prince Andrew stepped out, helped his small wife down, and let her enter the house ahead of him. Old Tikhon, wearing a wig, poked his head out of the antechamber door, whispered that the prince was sleeping, and quickly shut it again. Tikhon knew that neither the son's arrival nor any other unusual event was allowed to disturb the appointed order of the day. Prince Andrew apparently knew this just as well as Tikhon. He checked his watch, as if to confirm whether his father's habits had changed since his last visit, and, satisfied that they hadn't, turned to his wife.
Prince Andrew followed her with a courteous but melancholy expression.
They approached the sitting room door, from which the same passage of the sonata could be heard repeating. Prince Andrew stopped and made a pained face, as if bracing for something unpleasant.

The little princess walked in. The music broke off mid-phrase, a cry rang out, followed by Princess Mary's heavy footsteps and the sound of kissing. When Prince Andrew entered, the two princesses—who had met only once before, briefly, at his wedding—were locked in each other's arms, pressing their lips to whatever part of each other's face they could reach. Mademoiselle Bourienne stood nearby with her hand pressed to her heart, wearing a blissful smile and looking equally prepared to burst into tears or laughter. Prince Andrew shrugged and frowned, the way music lovers do when they hear a wrong note. The two women released each other, then immediately seized each other's hands again, kissing them, pulling them away, and kissing each other's faces once more. To Prince Andrew's bewilderment, they both began to cry, then kissed again. Mademoiselle Bourienne started crying too. Prince Andrew was clearly uncomfortable, but to the two women it all felt perfectly natural—it apparently never crossed their minds that their meeting could have gone any other way.
"And I had no idea!..." Princess Mary exclaimed. "Oh, Andrew—I didn't even see you."

Prince Andrew and his sister took each other's hands and kissed, and he told her she was still the same crybaby she had always been. Princess Mary turned toward her brother, and through her tears the warm, loving, gentle light of her large, luminous eyes—extraordinarily beautiful in that moment—rested on Prince Andrew's face.

The little princess chattered nonstop. Her short, downy upper lip kept dipping to meet her rosy lower lip, then lifting again as her face broke into a smile of gleaming teeth and sparkling eyes. She told them about an accident they'd had on Spassky Hill that could have been serious in her condition, then immediately reported that she'd left all her clothes in Petersburg and heaven knew what she would wear here, and that Andrew had completely changed, and that Kitty Odyntsova had married an old man, and that there was a real suitor for Mary—but they'd discuss that later. Princess Mary watched her brother in silence, her beautiful eyes full of love and sadness. She was clearly following her own train of thought, independent of her sister-in-law's stream of words. In the middle of a description of the latest Petersburg party, she turned to her brother:
"So you're really going to the war, Andrew?" she asked with a sigh.
"She needs to rest," Prince Andrew said with a frown. "Don't you, Lise? Take her to your room, and I'll go see Father. How is he? The same as ever?"

"Same hours? Same walks along the avenues? And the lathe?" Prince Andrew asked with a barely perceptible smile, showing that despite all his love and respect for his father, he was well aware of his quirks.

When the twenty minutes were up and it was time for the old prince to rise, Tikhon came to summon the young prince. In honor of his son's arrival, the old man made an exception to his routine: he gave orders for Prince Andrew to be admitted to his rooms while he dressed for dinner. The old prince always dressed in the old-fashioned way—an antique-style coat and powdered hair. When Prince Andrew entered his father's dressing room—not wearing the contemptuous expression he put on in drawing rooms, but the lively face he showed when talking with Pierre—the old man was sitting in a large leather armchair, wrapped in a powdering cape, offering his head to Tikhon's ministrations.

The old man was in high spirits after his pre-dinner nap. (He used to say that a nap after dinner was silver, but before dinner was gold.) He cast fond, sidelong glances at his son from beneath those thick, bushy brows. Prince Andrew went over and kissed his father on the indicated spot. He made no comment on his father's favorite hobby—ridiculing modern-day military leaders, and Bonaparte in particular.
"Yes, Father, I've come with my wife, who is expecting," Prince Andrew said, watching his father's face with eager, respectful attention. "How is your health?"
Prince Andrew smiled.

Prince Andrew, seeing his father wouldn't let it go, began reluctantly—but gradually with more and more animation, switching unconsciously from Russian to French as was his habit—to explain the campaign plan. He described how an army of ninety thousand was to threaten Prussia to force her out of neutrality and into the war; how part of that force would link up with Swedish troops at Stralsund; how two hundred and twenty thousand Austrians and a hundred thousand Russians would operate in Italy and on the Rhine; how fifty thousand Russians and an equal number of British would land at Naples; and how a combined force of five hundred thousand men was to attack the French from multiple directions. The old prince showed not the slightest interest during this explanation, continuing to dress and walk about as if he weren't listening. Three times he interrupted unexpectedly. Once he stopped the narrative by shouting: "The white one, the white one!"
The third interruption came as Prince Andrew was wrapping up. The old man began singing in the cracked voice of old age: [Speaking in French] "Marlborough is off to war. God knows when he'll return."

In the dining room—which, like every room in the house, had extraordinarily high ceilings—the household members and the footmen (one stationed behind each chair) stood waiting for the prince to appear. The head butler, napkin draped over his arm, was inspecting the table settings, signaling to the footmen, and glancing nervously between the clock and the door through which the prince would enter. Prince Andrew was studying a large gilt frame, new to him, that held the Bolkonsky family tree. Opposite it hung a matching frame with a poorly painted portrait—clearly the work of a local artist—of a prince in a crown, supposedly a descendant of Rurik and ancestor of the Bolkonskys. Prince Andrew looked again at the family tree, shook his head, and laughed the way one laughs at a portrait so perfectly capturing its subject that it becomes comical.
"Everyone has their weak spot," Prince Andrew continued. "Imagine—with his formidable intellect, indulging in this kind of vanity!"

"Well, Mikhail Ivanovich, things aren't looking good for our friend Bonaparte. Prince Andrew"—he always referred to his son this way—"has been telling me what forces are being gathered against him! And you and I never did think much of him."

The conversation turned again to the war, to Bonaparte, and to the generals and statesmen of the day. The old prince seemed convinced not only that every man of the current age was an infant who didn't know the ABCs of warfare or politics, and that Bonaparte was an insignificant little Frenchman who had succeeded only because there were no Potemkins or Suvorovs left to oppose him—but also that there were no real political difficulties in Europe and no real war, only a sort of puppet show in which the men of the day were playing at something serious. Prince Andrew cheerfully endured his father's mockery of modern leaders, drawing him out and listening with obvious enjoyment.

"Who told you that? Who?" the prince cried. "Suvorov!" He shoved his plate away—Tikhon caught it deftly. "Suvorov!... Think, Prince Andrew. Two great commanders—Frederick and Suvorov. Moreau!... Moreau would have been taken prisoner if Suvorov had been given a free hand. But he had the Austrian war council—the Hofskriegsratschnapswurst—on his back. The devil himself couldn't have managed them! When you get out there, you'll see what those councils are really like! Suvorov couldn't handle them—so what chance does Mikhail Kutuzov have? No, my boy," he continued, "you and your generals won't be a match for Bonaparte. You'll have to bring in the French so that birds of a feather can fight together. They've sent the German Pahlen to New York to fetch the Frenchman Moreau," he said, referring to the invitation extended that year for Moreau to enter Russian service. "Wonderful!... Were the Potemkins, Suvorovs, and Orlovs Germans? No, my boy—either you've all lost your minds, or I've outlived mine. God help you, and we'll see what happens. They've made Bonaparte into a great commander among them! Ha!..."
"I'm not saying all the plans are good," Prince Andrew said. "I'm just surprised by your opinion of Bonaparte. Laugh all you want, but Bonaparte is a great general all the same!"

"Listen," he said. "Don't worry about your wife — what can be done will be done. Now listen: give this letter to Mikhail Ilarionovich. I've written that he should put you to good use in real assignments and not keep you stuck as an adjutant — it's a dead-end position. Tell him I remember him and think well of him. And write to tell me how he receives you. If he treats you well, serve him. A son of Nicholas Bolkonski doesn't need to serve under anyone who's out of favor. Now come here."

"Very well. Now — goodbye!" He held out his hand for his son to kiss, then embraced him. "Remember this, Prince Andrew: if they kill you, it will grieve me — your old father..." He paused abruptly, then in a shrill, cracking voice suddenly cried out: "But if I learn that you did not conduct yourself as a son of Nicholas Bolkonski, I will be ashamed!"

But at that instant, a tall Austrian general in a greatcoat strode in quickly, slamming the door behind him. He wore the Order of Maria Theresa around his neck and had a black bandage wrapped around his head. He had obviously just arrived. Prince Andrew stopped short.

The Pavlograd Hussars were stationed two miles from Braunau. The squadron in which Nicholas Rostov served as a cadet was billeted in the German village of Salzeneck. The best quarters in the village had been assigned to the squadron commander, cavalry captain Denisov, known throughout the entire cavalry division as Vaska Denisov. Cadet Rostov had been living with the squadron commander ever since catching up with the regiment in Poland.

On the brow of the hill, among the field guns, the general commanding the rearguard stood with a staff officer, scanning the countryside through his field glass. A little behind them sat Nesvitsky, who had been sent to the rearguard by the commander in chief, perched on the trail of a gun carriage. A Cossack who accompanied him had handed over a knapsack and flask, and Nesvitsky was treating some officers to pies and genuine doppelkümmel liqueur. The officers had gathered around him gladly, some on their knees, others squatting cross-legged on the wet grass.
"Yes, the Austrian prince who built that castle was no fool. Lovely place! Why aren't you eating, gentlemen?" Nesvitsky was saying.
"I'm sure they will," said Nesvitsky. "No, but what I'd really love," he added, munching a pie with his moist-lipped, handsome mouth, "would be to slip in over there."
Nesvitsky heaved himself up, puffing, and walked over to the general with a smile.
"Shall I ride over there, your excellency?" Nesvitsky asked.
"Very good," Nesvitsky replied.

Two enemy shells had already flown across the bridge, where a crush of men was building up. Halfway across, Prince Nesvitsky had dismounted and now found his bulky body jammed against the railings. He glanced back, laughing, at the Cossack standing a few steps behind him holding two horses by their bridles. Every time Nesvitsky tried to push forward, soldiers and carts shoved him back against the railings, and all he could do was smile.

But the wagon driver paid no attention to the word "general" and shouted at the soldiers blocking his way. "Hey, boys! Keep to the left! Hold up!" But the soldiers, packed shoulder to shoulder with bayonets interlocking, moved across the bridge in a solid mass. Looking over the railing, Prince Nesvitsky watched the quick, noisy little waves of the Enns rippling and swirling around the bridge pilings, chasing one another downstream. Looking at the bridge itself, he saw an equally unbroken living wave of soldiers—shoulder straps, covered shakos, knapsacks, bayonets, long muskets, and beneath the shakos, faces with broad cheekbones, hollow cheeks, and dull, tired expressions—and feet trudging through the sticky mud that coated the bridge planks. Sometimes, through this monotonous stream of men, like a fleck of white foam on the river's current, an officer in a cloak, with a face of a different type, squeezed his way through. Sometimes, like a wood chip spinning in the water, a dismounted hussar, an orderly, or a civilian was carried along in the flood of infantry. And sometimes, like a log drifting downstream, an officers' or company baggage wagon—piled high, covered in leather, and hemmed in on every side—rolled across the bridge.
"Yeah, and that ham was delicious..." another replied with a loud laugh. And they too moved on, so that Nesvitsky never learned who had been hit in the teeth, or what ham had to do with any of it.

The girl smiled and took it. Nesvitsky, like every other man on the bridge, kept his eyes on the women until they had passed. When they were gone, the same stream of soldiers continued with the same kind of chatter, and finally everyone came to a halt. As so often happens, the horses pulling a supply wagon had balked at the end of the bridge, and the entire crowd was forced to wait.
Looking down at the waters of the Enns beneath the bridge, Nesvitsky suddenly heard a new sound—something approaching fast, something large that splashed into the water.
The crowd surged forward again. Nesvitsky realized it had been a cannonball.
"Nesvitsky! Nesvitsky, you blockhead!" came a hoarse voice from behind.

Nesvitsky turned and saw, about fifteen paces back but cut off by the solid, moving mass of infantry, Vaska Denisov—red-faced and shaggy, his cap shoved to the back of his black head, a cloak thrown dashingly over one shoulder.
"Vaska!" Nesvitsky called back joyfully. "What's going on?"
The soldiers crushed against each other with terrified faces, and Denisov managed to reach Nesvitsky.
"How is it you're not drunk today?" Nesvitsky asked when Denisov had ridden up alongside.
"What a dandy you look today!" said Nesvitsky, eyeing Denisov's new cloak and saddle cloth.
Denisov grinned, pulled a handkerchief from his sabretache that gave off a waft of perfume, and pressed it to Nesvitsky's nose.

The imposing bulk of Nesvitsky, trailed by his Cossack, combined with Denisov's fierce determination as he swung his sword and shouted like a madman, had such an effect that they managed to force their way through to the far side of the bridge and halt the infantry. At the bridgehead, Nesvitsky found the colonel he needed to deliver the order to, and having done so, rode back.

Nicholas Rostov turned away and gazed into the distance, as if searching for something—at the waters of the Danube, at the sky, at the sun. How beautiful the sky was: how blue, how calm, how deep! How bright and glorious the setting sun! How softly the distant waters of the Danube glittered! And more beautiful still were the far-off blue mountains beyond the river, the convent, the mysterious gorges, the pine forests veiled in mist at their summits... There was peace there, and happiness... "I would want nothing else, nothing at all, if only I were there," Rostov thought. "In me alone and in that sunshine there is so much happiness. But here... groans, suffering, fear, and this chaos and rush... Over there—they're shouting again, and again everyone is running somewhere, and I'll run with them, and it—death—is here, above me and all around me... One more instant, and I will never again see this sun, this water, that gorge!..."

Prince Andrew had served during the battle as aide to the Austrian General Schmidt, who was killed in the action. His horse had been shot from under him and a bullet had grazed his arm. As a mark of the commander in chief's special favor, he was chosen to carry the news of this victory to the Austrian court, which was now at Brünn rather than Vienna, since Vienna was threatened by the French. Despite his seemingly delicate build, Prince Andrew could endure physical hardship far better than many much stronger men. On the night of the battle, having arrived at Krems excited but not tired, with dispatches from Dokhturov for Kutuzov, he was immediately sent on with a special dispatch to Brünn. Being chosen for such a mission meant not only a reward but an important step toward promotion.

The night was dark but starry. The road showed black against the snow that had fallen the day before—the day of the battle. Replaying his impressions of the recent fight, pleasantly imagining the reaction his news of victory would produce, remembering the send-off from the commander in chief and his fellow officers, Prince Andrew raced along in a post chaise, savoring the feelings of a man who has finally begun to achieve a long-desired happiness. As soon as he closed his eyes, his ears filled with the rattle of wheels and the sensation of victory. Then he would start imagining that the Russians were fleeing and that he himself had been killed—but he quickly shook off the vision with a surge of joy, as if discovering all over again that none of it was true, that on the contrary, it was the French who had fled. He recalled every detail of the victory once more, and his own steady courage during the battle, and feeling reassured, he drifted off to sleep... The dark, starry night gave way to a bright, cheerful morning. The snow was melting in the sunshine, the horses galloped briskly, and on both sides of the road stretched forests of different kinds, fields, and villages.

Prince Andrew told his driver to stop and asked a soldier which battle they had been wounded in. "Day before yesterday, on the Danube," the soldier answered. Prince Andrew took out his purse and gave the man three gold coins.

It was already quite dark by the time Prince Andrew rattled over the cobblestone streets of Brünn and found himself surrounded by tall buildings, the glow of shop windows and house lamps, elegant carriages, and all the bustle of a large, lively city—always so appealing to a soldier after life in camp. Despite his rapid journey and sleepless night, he felt even more energized and alert as he pulled up to the palace than he had the day before. Only his eyes had a feverish gleam, and his thoughts followed one another with extraordinary speed and clarity. He relived the details of the battle once more—no longer hazy, but sharp and precise, framed in the concise form in which he imagined reporting them to Emperor Francis. He vividly anticipated the offhand questions that might be asked and the answers he would give. He expected to be ushered into the Emperor's presence immediately. At the main entrance to the palace, however, an official hurried out to meet him and, learning that he was a special messenger, directed him to a different entrance.

The adjutant on duty met Prince Andrew, asked him to wait, and went in to see the minister. Five minutes later he returned and, bowing with exaggerated courtesy, led Prince Andrew along a corridor to the room where the Minister of War was working. The adjutant's elaborate politeness seemed designed to discourage any attempt at familiarity from the Russian messenger.

Prince Andrew's elated mood dimmed considerably as he approached the minister's door. He felt slighted, and without being fully aware of it, his sense of offense immediately hardened into a disdain that was entirely uncalled for. His quick mind instantly supplied a perspective that gave him the right to look down on both the adjutant and the minister. "Far from the smell of gunpowder, they probably think winning victories is easy!" he thought. His eyes narrowed scornfully as he entered the Minister of War's room with deliberately measured steps. This feeling of contempt only deepened when he saw the minister seated at a large table, reading documents and marking them with pencil notes, paying no attention whatsoever to his arrival for the first two or three minutes. A wax candle stood on either side of the minister's bent, bald head with its gray temples. He went on reading to the end without looking up at the sound of the door opening and footsteps approaching.

Prince Andrew felt that either Kutuzov's army interested the Minister of War less than the other matters on his desk, or the minister wanted to give that impression. "But it makes absolutely no difference to me," he thought. The minister gathered the remaining papers, straightened them into a neat pile, and finally raised his head. He had a distinctive, intelligent face—but the moment he turned to Prince Andrew, its firm, perceptive expression shifted in a way that was clearly deliberate and habitual. His face assumed the stupid, artificial smile—making no attempt whatsoever to disguise its falseness—of a man who spends his days receiving one petitioner after another.
Having skimmed the dispatch, he laid it on the table and studied Prince Andrew, clearly turning something over in his mind.

When Prince Andrew left the palace, he felt that all the excitement and happiness the victory had given him had been surrendered into the indifferent hands of the Minister of War and the polite adjutant. The entire character of his thoughts changed in an instant; the battle now seemed like the memory of some distant event, long past.
Prince Andrew stayed in Brünn with Bilibin, a Russian he knew from the diplomatic service.

"Ah, my dear Prince! I couldn't ask for a more welcome guest," said Bilibin, coming out to meet Prince Andrew. "Franz, put the prince's things in my bedroom," he told the servant who was showing Bolkonsky in. "So you're a bearer of victory news? Wonderful! And here I am sitting around sick, as you can see."
After washing and changing, Prince Andrew came into the diplomat's luxurious study and sat down to the dinner that had been prepared for him. Bilibin settled himself comfortably by the fire.

Bilibin was a thirty-five-year-old bachelor who moved in the same circles as Prince Andrew. They'd known each other previously in Petersburg but had become closer when Prince Andrew was in Vienna with Kutuzov. Just as Prince Andrew was a young man who showed every sign of rising high in the military, so Bilibin—to an even greater extent—showed every sign of rising in the diplomatic world. He was still young but no longer a novice diplomat, having entered the service at sixteen and served in Paris and Copenhagen before landing a fairly important post in Vienna. Both the foreign minister and the Russian ambassador in Vienna knew him and valued him. He wasn't one of those many diplomats who are respected merely because they have certain negative qualities, avoid doing certain things, and speak French. He was one of those who genuinely enjoyed work and knew how to do it well, and despite his natural laziness would sometimes spend an entire night at his desk. He worked well regardless of the subject matter. It wasn't the question "What for?" but "How?" that interested him. He didn't particularly care what a diplomatic matter was about, but it gave him enormous pleasure to craft a circular, memorandum, or report with skill, precision, and elegance. Bilibin's services were valued not only for his writing but also for his ability to deal and converse with people in the highest spheres.

Bilibin enjoyed conversation the way he enjoyed work—only when it could be made elegantly witty. In society he was always waiting for a chance to say something memorable and only joined a conversation when such an opportunity arose. His talk was always laced with cleverly original, polished phrases of general interest. These sayings were prepared in the inner workshop of his mind in portable form, as if designed so that minor society figures could carry them from one drawing room to the next. And indeed, Bilibin's witticisms circulated through the Viennese salons and often had an influence on matters considered important.
Bolkonsky, very modestly and without once mentioning himself, described the battle and his reception by the Minister of War.
Bilibin smiled and the wrinkles on his face disappeared.
"And why didn't you get there at seven in the morning? You should have been there by seven," returned Bilibin with a smile. "You should have been there at seven in the morning."

"I know," interrupted Bilibin, "you're thinking it's very easy to capture marshals while sitting on a sofa by the fire! That's true enough, but still—why didn't you capture him? So don't be surprised if not only the Minister of War but also His Most August Majesty Emperor and King Francis isn't exactly thrilled by your victory. Even I, a lowly secretary of the Russian Embassy, feel no need to celebrate by giving my Franz a coin or letting him go off to the Prater with his sweetheart... Though of course, we don't have a Prater here."

"Now it's my turn to ask you 'why?' my dear fellow," said Bolkonsky. "I confess I don't understand—perhaps there are diplomatic subtleties here beyond my humble intelligence—but I can't make sense of it. Mack loses an entire army, Archduke Ferdinand and Archduke Karl show no signs of life and blunder after blunder. Kutuzov alone wins a real victory, breaking the spell of French invincibility, and the Minister of War doesn't even want to hear the details."
After the exhaustion of the journey, his reception, and especially after dinner, Bolkonsky found he could not fully grasp the significance of what he was hearing.

"Count Lichtenfels was here this morning," Bilibin continued, "and showed me a letter describing the French parade through Vienna in full detail: Prince Murat and the whole spectacle... So you see, your victory is hardly cause for celebration, and you can't expect to be received as a savior."

"Well, I think it is. The big men here think so too, but they don't dare say it. It will be as I said at the start of the campaign: it won't be your skirmish at Dürrenstein, or gunpowder at all, that decides this—but the people who planned it," said Bilibin, quoting one of his own bon mots, releasing the wrinkles on his forehead, and pausing. "The only question now is what comes of the meeting between Emperor Alexander and the King of Prussia in Berlin. If Prussia joins the allies, Austria's hand will be forced and there will be war. If not, it's just a matter of deciding where to draw up the terms of the new Campo Formio."

"Bonaparte?" said Bilibin inquiringly, wrinkling his forehead to signal that a witticism was coming. "Buonaparte?" he repeated, stressing the 'u.' "I think, however, now that he's laying down the law for Austria at Schönbrunn, we really must drop the 'u.' I shall certainly adopt the innovation and simply call him Bonaparte!"
[Bilibin's joke: "We must let him off the 'u'!" — a pun on the French spelling of Buonaparte vs. Bonaparte.]
"If we live, we'll see," replied Bilibin, his face becoming smooth again—a sign the conversation was over.

The next day he woke late. As his recent impressions came flooding back, the first thought in his mind was that today he had to be presented to Emperor Francis. He remembered the Minister of War, the courteous Austrian adjutant, Bilibin, and last night's conversation. Having dressed in full parade uniform—which he hadn't worn in a long time—he went into Bilibin's study looking fresh, lively, and handsome, with his hand still bandaged. Four gentlemen from the diplomatic corps were already in the study. Prince Andrew was already acquainted with Prince Hippolyte Kuragin, who served as a secretary to the embassy. Bilibin introduced him to the others.

The gentlemen gathered at Bilibin's were young, wealthy, fashionable men who formed a special circle both here and in Vienna. Bilibin, their leader, called the group "ours." This set, made up almost entirely of diplomats, clearly had its own interests that had nothing to do with war or politics but revolved around high society, certain women, and the ceremonial side of government service. These gentlemen welcomed Prince Andrew as one of their own—an honor they extended to very few. Out of politeness, and to start a conversation, they asked him a few questions about the army and the battle, but then the talk quickly turned to lighthearted jokes and gossip.
"But the worst of it, gentlemen—and I'm giving Kuragin away here—is that the man is genuinely suffering, and this Don Juan, this scoundrel, is taking advantage of it!"

"You don't know this yet, Bolkonsky," said Bilibin, turning to Prince Andrew, "but all the horrors committed by the French army—I almost said the Russian army—are nothing compared to what this man has been doing to the women here!"

Bilibin and the rest of "ours" burst out laughing right in Hippolyte's face, and Prince Andrew saw that Hippolyte—of whom, he had to admit, he had nearly been jealous on his wife's account—was the group's favorite target.
"Oh, I have to give you a treat," Bilibin whispered to Bolkonsky. "Kuragin is priceless when he talks politics—you have to see how serious he gets!"

"Wait, I'm not finished..." he said to Prince Andrew, grabbing him by the arm. "I believe that intervention will prove stronger than non-intervention. And..." He paused. "Finally, one cannot attribute the non-receipt of our dispatch of November eighteenth. That is how it will end." And he released Bolkonsky's arm to show he had quite finished.
"Demosthenes, I recognize you by the pebble hidden in your golden mouth!" said Bilibin, and the tuft of hair on his head bobbed with satisfaction.

"Well then, gentlemen," said Bilibin, "Bolkonsky is my guest here in this house and in Brünn itself. I want to show him the best time I can, with all the pleasures life here has to offer. If we were in Vienna it would be easy, but here in this miserable Moravian backwater it's harder, and I'm asking all of you to help me. You can handle the theater, I'll take care of society, and you, Hippolyte—the women, naturally."
"In general, we need to convert this bloodthirsty soldier to more civilized pursuits," said Bilibin.
"Well, goodbye, Bolkonsky! Goodbye, Prince! Come back early for dinner," called several voices. "We'll look after you."
"When you're speaking with the Emperor, try to say good things about the supply situation and the route planning," said Bilibin, walking him to the hall.
"I'd like to speak well of them, but as far as I know the facts, I can't," replied Bolkonsky with a smile.

At the levee, Prince Andrew stood among the Austrian officers as instructed, and Emperor Francis merely stared fixedly at his face and gave a slight nod with his long head. But after it was over, the adjutant he'd seen the day before ceremoniously informed Bolkonsky that the Emperor wished to grant him an audience. Emperor Francis received him standing in the middle of the room. Before the conversation began, Prince Andrew was struck by the fact that the Emperor seemed flustered and kept blushing, as if he didn't know what to say.

Prince Andrew answered. Then came more questions, equally straightforward: "Was Kutuzov in good health? When had he left Krems?" The Emperor spoke as though his only goal were to get through a set number of questions—the answers, quite obviously, didn't interest him.

"I cannot inform Your Majesty at what time the battle began at the front lines, but at Dürrenstein, where I was stationed, our attack began after five in the afternoon," replied Bolkonsky, growing more animated and expecting he might finally have the chance to give a reliable account—which he had prepared in his mind—of all he knew and had seen. But the Emperor smiled and cut him off.

Contrary to Bilibin's prediction, the news Prince Andrew had brought was received with joy. A thanksgiving service was arranged, Kutuzov was awarded the Grand Cross of Maria Theresa, and the entire army received decorations. Bolkonsky was invited everywhere and had to spend the whole morning making calls on the leading Austrian dignitaries. Between four and five in the afternoon, having completed all his calls, he was walking back to Bilibin's house, composing in his head a letter to his father about the battle and his visit to Brünn. At the door he found a carriage half-loaded with luggage. Franz, Bilibin's servant, was struggling to drag a heavy trunk out through the front door.
Before returning to Bilibin's, Prince Andrew had stopped at a bookshop to stock up on books for the campaign and had spent some time browsing.
Bilibin came out to meet him. His usually calm face showed excitement.
Bolkonsky shrugged.

"That's precisely the situation," answered Bilibin. "Listen. The French entered Vienna as I told you. Fine. The next day—which was yesterday—these gentlemen, the marshals Murat, Lannes, and Belliard, mount their horses and ride to the bridge. (Note that all three are Gascons.) 'Gentlemen,' says one of them, 'you know the Thabor Bridge is mined and double-mined, that there are serious fortifications at the bridgehead, and that fifteen thousand men have orders to blow it up and keep us from crossing. But it would please our sovereign Emperor Napoleon if we took this bridge, so let's go take it!' 'Yes, let's!' say the others. And off they go and take the bridge, cross it, and now their entire army is on this side of the Danube, marching toward us—toward you, and your supply lines."

The moment he learned that the Russian army was in such a desperate position, it occurred to him that he was the one destined to lead it out of this crisis—that here was the Toulon that would lift him from the ranks of obscure officers and offer him his first step toward glory! As he listened to Bilibin, he was already imagining how, upon reaching the army, he would present an opinion at the war council—the only plan that could save them—and how he alone would be entrusted with carrying it out.

"I'm not joking," Bilibin went on. "Nothing could be more true or more tragic. These gentlemen ride onto the bridge alone, waving white handkerchiefs. They assure the officer on duty that they, the marshals, are on their way to negotiate with Prince Auersperg. He lets them into the bridgehead. They spin a thousand tall tales, saying the war is over, that Emperor Francis is arranging a meeting with Bonaparte, that they'd like to see Prince Auersperg, and so on. The officer sends for Auersperg. The gentlemen embrace the Austrian officers, crack jokes, sit on the cannons, and meanwhile a French battalion slips onto the bridge unnoticed, throws the detonation charges into the water, and reaches the fortifications. At last the lieutenant general himself appears—our dear Prince Auersperg von Mautern. 'Dearest enemy! Flower of the Austrian army! Hero of the Turkish wars! Hostilities are over, we can shake hands... Emperor Napoleon burns with impatience to make Prince Auersperg's acquaintance.' In short, these gentlemen—true Gascons—so bewildered him with their fine words, and he was so flattered by his sudden intimacy with the French marshals, and so dazzled by the sight of Murat's cloak and ostrich plumes, that he couldn't see what was right in front of him—and forgot he was supposed to be firing on the enemy!" Despite his animated delivery, Bilibin didn't forget to pause after this bon mot to let it land. "The French battalion rushes the bridgehead, spikes the guns, and the bridge is taken! But the best part," he continued, his excitement subsiding under the pleasant momentum of his own story, "is that the sergeant in charge of the cannon—the one meant to give the signal to detonate the mines—seeing the French troops swarming onto the bridge, was about to fire. But Lannes grabbed his hand. The sergeant, who was clearly smarter than his general, went up to Auersperg and said: 'Prince, you're being deceived—these are the French!' Murat, seeing that all was lost if the sergeant was allowed to speak, turned to Auersperg with a look of feigned astonishment—a true Gascon—and said: 'I hardly recognize the world-famous Austrian discipline when you allow a subordinate to address you like that!' It was a stroke of genius. Prince Auersperg, feeling his authority challenged, ordered the sergeant arrested. Come on, you have to admit this Thabor Bridge business is magnificent! It's not exactly stupidity, and it's not exactly treachery either..."

"Not that either. That would put the court in too bad a light," replied Bilibin. "It's not treachery, not villainy, not stupidity—it's just like Ulm... it's..." He seemed to be searching for the right expression. "It's... it's a case of Mack. We've been Macked," he concluded, feeling he had produced a fresh witticism that would make the rounds. His previously furrowed brow smoothed out with pleasure, and with a slight smile he began examining his nails.
"You know, my dear fellow," said Bilibin, following him, "I've been thinking about you. Why are you going?"
"Stop joking, Bilibin," said Bolkonsky.

"I'm speaking sincerely, as a friend! Think about it. Where are you going, and why, when you could stay here? You're facing one of two outcomes"—and the skin over his left temple puckered—"either you won't reach your regiment before peace is concluded, or you'll share in the defeat and disgrace of Kutuzov's entire army."
And Bilibin smoothed his temple, feeling his dilemma was unanswerable.
"My dear fellow, you are a hero!" said Bilibin.

That same night, after taking leave of the Minister of War, Bolkonsky set off to rejoin the army, not knowing where he would find it and fearing he might be captured by the French on the way to Krems.
"Here's our beloved Orthodox Russian army," thought Bolkonsky, remembering Bilibin's words.
He turned around. Nesvitsky's handsome face was looking out of a small window. Nesvitsky, chewing something and moving his moist lips, was waving his arm and calling him over.
"Bolkonsky! Bolkonsky! Can't you hear me? Come here, quickly!" he shouted.

Going inside, Prince Andrew found Nesvitsky and another adjutant eating. They spun around to face him, asking if he had any news. On their familiar faces he read alarm and anxiety. This was especially striking on Nesvitsky's face, which was usually so cheerful.
"Where is the commander in chief?" asked Bolkonsky.
"Well, is it true? Peace and surrender?" asked Nesvitsky.
"And us, my dear fellow! It's terrible! I was wrong to laugh at Mack—we're getting it even worse," said Nesvitsky. "But sit down and have something to eat."

"Well, I've managed to pack everything I need onto two horses," said Nesvitsky. "They made up excellent packs for me—good enough to cross the Bohemian mountains. Things look grim, old friend! But what's wrong with you? You must be sick—you're shivering like that," he added, noticing Prince Andrew flinch as if from an electric shock.
"I can't make it out at all," said Nesvitsky.

Passing Kutuzov's carriage and the exhausted saddle horses of his entourage, with their Cossacks talking loudly together, Prince Andrew entered the hallway. Kutuzov himself, he was told, was inside with Prince Bagration and Weyrother—the Austrian general who had replaced Schmidt. In the corridor, little Kozlovsky was squatting on his heels in front of a clerk. The clerk, with his sleeves rolled up, was scribbling furiously on an overturned tub. Kozlovsky's face looked haggard—he clearly hadn't slept all night either. He glanced at Prince Andrew without so much as a nod.
"Can't write that fast, Your Honor," said the clerk, looking up at Kozlovsky with irritation and disrespect.

Through the door came the sounds of Kutuzov's voice—agitated and unhappy—broken by another voice, one Prince Andrew didn't recognize. From the sound of these voices, from Kozlovsky's distracted expression, from the clerk's rudeness, from the fact that both Kozlovsky and the clerk were squatting on the floor by a tub so close to the commander in chief, and from the noisy laughter of the Cossacks holding the horses by the window—from all of this, Prince Andrew sensed that something critical and catastrophic was about to happen.
He turned to Kozlovsky with urgent questions.
"One moment, Prince," said Kozlovsky. "Orders for Bagration."

Prince Andrew moved toward the door where the voices were coming from. Just as he was about to open it, the voices fell silent, the door swung open, and Kutuzov appeared in the doorway with his eagle nose and puffy face. Prince Andrew stood directly in front of him, but the expression in the commander in chief's one good eye showed he was so consumed by thoughts and worries that he didn't even register who was standing there. He stared straight at his adjutant's face without recognizing him.
"Well, have you finished?" he said to Kozlovsky.
Bagration, a lean middle-aged man of medium height with a firm, impassive face of Eastern features, emerged behind the commander in chief.
"I have the honor to present myself," said Prince Andrew, louder this time, holding out an envelope to Kutuzov.
Kutuzov walked out to the porch with Bagration.
"Well, goodbye, Prince," he said to Bagration. "My blessing, and may Christ be with you in your great endeavor!"

His face suddenly softened and tears welled in his eyes. With his left hand he drew Bagration toward him, and with his right—on which he wore a ring—he made the sign of the cross over him in what was clearly a habitual gesture, offering his puffy cheek. But Bagration kissed him on the neck instead.
"Christ be with you!" Kutuzov repeated, and turned toward his carriage. "Get in with me," he said to Bolkonsky.
"Your Excellency, I would like to be of use here. Allow me to stay with Prince Bagration's detachment."
"Get in," said Kutuzov, and when he noticed Bolkonsky still hesitating, he added: "I need good officers myself. Need them myself!"

"There is still much, much ahead of us," he said with the penetrating insight of an old man who seemed to understand everything passing through Bolkonsky's mind. "If even a tenth of his detachment comes back, I shall thank God," he added, as if speaking to himself.

Prince Andrew glanced at Kutuzov's face, only a foot away, and found his eyes drawn to the carefully washed seams of the scar near his temple where a bullet had pierced his skull at Ismail, and to the empty eye socket. "Yes, he has earned the right to speak so calmly about those men's deaths," thought Bolkonsky.

Kutuzov did not answer. He seemed to have forgotten what he'd been saying and sat sunk in thought. Five minutes later, swaying gently on the soft springs of the carriage, he turned to Prince Andrew. There was not a trace of emotion on his face. With subtle irony, he began questioning Prince Andrew about the details of his interview with the Emperor, about the remarks he'd heard at court regarding the Krems affair, and about certain ladies they both knew.

On November 1st, Kutuzov had received intelligence from a spy that the army he commanded was in a nearly hopeless situation. The spy reported that the French, having crossed the bridge at Vienna, were advancing in massive force toward Kutuzov's line of communication with the reinforcements arriving from Russia. If Kutuzov chose to remain at Krems, Napoleon's army of a hundred and fifty thousand men would completely cut him off and surround his exhausted force of forty thousand—and he would find himself in the same position as Mack at Ulm. If he chose to abandon the road connecting him with the approaching Russian reinforcements, he would have to march without roads into the unknown terrain of the Bohemian mountains, fighting off a superior enemy while giving up all hope of linking up with Buxhöwden. If he chose to retreat along the road from Krems to Olmütz to join the incoming Russian troops, he risked being overtaken on that road by the French who had crossed the Vienna bridge—and burdened by his baggage and supply trains, he would have to fight on the march against an enemy three times his strength attacking from two directions.
Kutuzov chose this last option.

The French, according to the spy, had crossed the Vienna bridge and were making forced marches toward Znaim, which lay sixty-six miles along Kutuzov's line of retreat. If he reached Znaim before the French, there was real hope of saving the army. If the French got there first, the entire army faced either the kind of humiliation Mack had suffered at Ulm, or total annihilation. But it was impossible for Kutuzov to reach Znaim ahead of the French with his whole army. The French road from Vienna to Znaim was shorter and better than the Russian road from Krems to Znaim.

The night he received this intelligence, Kutuzov sent Bagration's advance guard—four thousand men—to the right, across the hills from the Krems-Znaim road to the Vienna-Znaim road. Bagration was to make this march without stopping to rest and to take up a position facing Vienna with Znaim at his back. If he managed to get there ahead of the French, he was to hold them off for as long as possible. Kutuzov himself, with the rest of the army and all the supply trains, took the road to Znaim.

Marching thirty miles through a stormy night across trackless hills, with hungry, poorly shod soldiers, and losing a third of his men as stragglers along the way, Bagration reached the Vienna-Znaim road at Hollabrünn a few hours ahead of the French approaching from Vienna. Kutuzov and his supply trains still had several days of marching before they could reach Znaim. So Bagration, with his four thousand hungry, exhausted men, would have to hold off the entire enemy army for days at Hollabrünn—which was clearly impossible. But a twist of fate made the impossible possible. The success of the trick that had handed the Vienna bridge to the French without a fight led Murat to try deceiving Kutuzov in the same way. When Murat encountered Bagration's small detachment on the Znaim road, he mistook it for Kutuzov's entire army. To ensure he could crush it completely, he waited for the rest of his troops still coming from Vienna, and in the meantime offered a three-day truce on the condition that both armies hold their positions without moving. Murat declared that peace negotiations were already underway, and that he was therefore proposing the truce to avoid unnecessary bloodshed. Count Nostitz, the Austrian general commanding the forward positions, believed Murat's envoy and pulled back, leaving Bagration's division exposed. Another envoy rode to the Russian lines to announce the peace talks and offer the Russian army a three-day truce. Bagration replied that he had no authority to accept or reject a truce and sent his adjutant to Kutuzov to report the offer.

A truce was Kutuzov's only chance to buy time, give Bagration's worn-out troops some rest, and let the baggage and heavy supply trains—whose movements were hidden from the French—advance at least one more stage toward Znaim. The truce offer was the only chance, and a completely unexpected one, of saving the army. As soon as he received the news, Kutuzov immediately dispatched Adjutant General Wintzingerode to the enemy camp. Wintzingerode was not merely to agree to the truce but also to propose terms of surrender—and meanwhile, Kutuzov sent his adjutants racing back to push the movement of the entire army's baggage trains along the Krems-Znaim road as fast as possible. Bagration's exhausted and hungry detachment, which alone was covering the movement of the supply trains and the whole army, had to remain in place facing an enemy eight times its size.

Kutuzov's expectation—that the surrender proposal (which committed him to nothing) would buy time for part of the transport to get through, and that Murat's mistake would soon be discovered—proved correct. As soon as Bonaparte, who was at Schönbrunn sixteen miles from Hollabrünn, received Murat's dispatch with the proposed truce and surrender terms, he saw through the ruse and wrote the following letter to Murat:

Bonaparte's adjutant rode at full gallop with this furious letter to Murat. Bonaparte himself, not trusting his generals, moved out with the entire Guard toward the battlefield, determined not to let a ready victim escape. And Bagration's four thousand men, meanwhile, cheerfully lit their campfires, dried and warmed themselves, and cooked porridge for the first time in three days—not one of them knowing or imagining what awaited them.
"These are the pleasures of camp life, Prince."

Another company, a lucky one since not every unit had vodka, was gathered around a pockmarked, broad-shouldered sergeant major who tilted a small keg, filling one by one the canteen lids held out to him. The soldiers raised the lids to their lips with something like reverence, drained them, swished the vodka around in their mouths, and walked away with brightened faces, licking their lips and wiping them on the sleeves of their greatcoats. Every face was as calm as if all this were happening back home during a peaceful camp, not within sight of the enemy before a battle in which at least half of them would fall. After passing a chasseur regiment and the Kiev grenadiers—fine men busy with similar peaceful routines—near the regimental commander's shelter, which was taller and different from the rest, Prince Andrew came upon a platoon of grenadiers in front of whom a naked man lay on the ground. Two soldiers held him down while two others lashed his bare back with switches. The man screamed in an unnatural, animal way. A heavy-set major paced up and down the line, ignoring the screams, and kept repeating:
"They'll make you dance."
"What's he singing about?"

The regimental commander, a thin, frail-looking old man with a kind smile—his drooping eyelids covering more than half his eyes and giving him a gentle expression—rode up to Bagration and greeted him like a host welcoming an honored guest. He reported that his regiment had been attacked by French cavalry, and that although the attack had been repulsed, he'd lost more than half his men. He used the military term "repulsed" to describe what had happened, but in truth he did not himself know what had happened during that half hour to the troops entrusted to him, and could not say with certainty whether the attack had been repulsed or his regiment had been broken up. All he really knew was that at the start of the action, shells and bullets had begun flying all over his regiment, hitting his men. Then someone had shouted "Cavalry!" and his soldiers had started shooting. They were still shooting now—not at the cavalry, which had vanished, but at French infantry that had moved into the hollow and was firing at them. Prince Bagration nodded, as though this was precisely what he'd expected. Turning to his adjutant, he ordered him to bring down the two battalions of the Sixth Chasseurs they'd just passed. Prince Andrew was struck by the change in Bagration's expression at that moment. His face now showed the focused, joyful determination you see in a man who, on a sweltering day, takes one final running start before plunging into the water. The dull, sleepy look was gone, and so was the pretense of deep deliberation. His round, steady, hawklike eyes stared ahead with eager, almost disdainful intensity, fixing on nothing in particular, though his movements remained slow and measured.

Old Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky received a letter from Prince Vasili in November 1805, announcing that he and his son would be visiting. 'I'm going on an inspection tour, and of course I won't mind an extra seventy miles to see you, my esteemed benefactor,' wrote Prince Vasili. 'My son Anatole is traveling with me on his way to the army, so I hope you'll allow him to personally express the deep respect that, following his father's example, he feels for you.'
"Come here, Rostov. Let's drink to drown our sorrows!" shouted Denisov, who had settled by the roadside with a flask and some food.
Rostov saw tears filling the Emperor's eyes and heard him say to Czartoryski as he rode off: "What a terrible thing war is — what a terrible thing! Quelle terrible chose que la guerre!"

Just as in a clock's mechanism, so in the mechanism of the military machine: once an impulse is given, it leads inevitably to the final result. Wheels creak on their axles as the cogs engage one another and the revolving pulleys whir with the rapidity of their movement, but a neighboring wheel is as quiet and motionless as though it were prepared to remain so for a hundred years. And just as the untouched parts of a clock sit completely still until the motion reaches them — wheels that could remain idle for a hundred years — so it is in an army. But the moment comes when the lever catches, and that dormant wheel begins to creak and joins the common motion, the ultimate result and purpose of which are beyond its comprehension.

At eight o'clock, Kutuzov rode toward Pratzen at the head of the fourth column — Miloradovich's — which was supposed to replace the columns of Przhebyshevsky and Langeron, both of which had already descended into the valley. He greeted the soldiers of the lead regiment and gave the order to march, signaling that he intended to lead this column himself. When they reached the village of Pratzen, he halted. Prince Andrew rode behind, lost among the enormous crowd that made up the commander in chief's retinue. Confused and swelling crowds were streaming back toward the place where, just five minutes earlier, the troops had marched past the Emperors. The troops were running in such a dense mass that once you were caught among them, it was nearly impossible to get free. One man was shouting, "Move! Why are you blocking us?" Having also fought his way out of the flood of fugitives, Prince Andrew tried to keep close to Kutuzov. Through the smoke on the hillside, he could see a Russian battery still firing, with French soldiers running toward it. Higher up stood Russian infantry that was neither advancing to protect the battery nor retreating with the fleeing crowd. A mounted general broke away from the infantry and rode up to Kutuzov. Of his original suite, only four men remained. They were all pale, exchanging silent looks.
But before he had finished speaking, Prince Andrew — tears of shame and fury choking him — had already leapt from his horse and was running toward the standard.
"Hurrah!" Prince Andrew shouted, and barely able to hold up the heavy standard, he ran forward, fully confident that the entire battalion would follow him.

And indeed, he ran only a few steps alone. First one soldier moved, then another, and soon the whole battalion charged forward with a shout of "Hurrah!" and overtook him. A sergeant ran up and grabbed the flag, which was swaying from its weight in Prince Andrew's hands, but he was killed immediately. Prince Andrew seized the standard again and, dragging it by the staff, ran on with the battalion. Ahead he could see Russian artillerymen — some still fighting, others abandoning their guns and running toward him. He could also see French infantry soldiers seizing the artillery horses and turning the cannons around. Prince Andrew and the battalion were now within twenty paces of the guns. He heard the ceaseless whistle of bullets above him, and to his right and left soldiers kept groaning and falling. But he didn't look at them — he looked only at what was happening in front of him, at the battery. He could now clearly see a red-haired gunner with his cap knocked crooked, pulling one end of a ramrod while a French soldier tugged at the other. He could distinctly see the frantic yet angry expressions on both men's faces — they clearly had no idea what they were doing.

"What are they even doing?" Prince Andrew wondered, watching them. "Why doesn't the red-haired gunner run? He's unarmed. Why doesn't the Frenchman stab him? The gunner won't get away before the Frenchman remembers his bayonet and runs him through."

And sure enough, another French soldier came running up with his musket trailing behind him, heading straight for the two struggling men. The fate of the red-haired gunner — who had triumphantly secured the ramrod and still had no idea what was about to happen to him — was about to be decided. But Prince Andrew never saw how it ended. It felt as though one of the soldiers near him struck him on the head with the full swing of a club. It hurt, but what was worse was that the pain broke his concentration and kept him from seeing what he had been watching.

"What's this? Am I falling? My legs are giving way," he thought — and fell onto his back. He opened his eyes, hoping to see how the fight between the Frenchmen and the gunners had ended, whether the red-haired gunner had been killed, whether the cannon had been captured or saved. But he saw nothing. Above him now there was only the sky — the vast sky, not clear, yet immeasurably high, with gray clouds drifting slowly across it. "How quiet, how peaceful, how solemn — nothing like the way I was running," Prince Andrew thought. "Not the way we ran, shouting and fighting — not like the gunner and the Frenchman clawing at the ramrod with their frightened, angry faces. The clouds moving across that endless sky — how completely different they are from all of that. How is it I never noticed this sky before? And how happy I am to have found it at last! Yes! Everything is empty, everything is a lie — except this infinite sky. Nothing exists, nothing at all, except this. But even the sky doesn't really exist — there is nothing but stillness and peace. Thank God!"

The discussions dragged on, and the longer they lasted, the more heated the disputes became — culminating in shouts and personal attacks — and the less possible it was to reach any general conclusion. Prince Andrew, listening to this babel of languages and to these conjectures, plans, refutations, and outbursts, felt nothing but amazement at what they were all saying. A thought that had long since and often occurred to him during his military service — the idea that there is not and cannot be any science of war, and that therefore there can be no such thing as military genius — now struck him as an obvious truth. "What theory and science can apply to a matter whose conditions and circumstances are unknown and cannot be defined, especially when the strength of the forces involved cannot be measured? No one was or is able to foresee what position our army or the enemy's will be in tomorrow, and no one can gauge the real strength of any given detachment. Sometimes — when there is no coward at the front to shout 'We're cut off!' and start running, but instead a brave and cheerful fellow who shouts 'Hurrah!' — a force of five thousand is worth thirty thousand, as at Schön Grabern, while at other times fifty thousand flee from eight thousand, as at Austerlitz. What science can govern a matter in which, as in all practical affairs, nothing can be precisely determined and everything depends on countless conditions whose significance reveals itself only at a particular moment that no one can predict? Armfeldt says our army is cut in half, and Paulucci says we have the French between two fires; Michaud says the Drissa camp is worthless because the river is behind it, while Pfuel says that is exactly what makes it strong; Toll proposes one plan, Armfeldt another — and they are all good and all bad, because the merits of any proposal can only be seen at the moment of execution. And why do they all talk of 'military genius'? Is a man a genius because he can order bread to be brought up at the right time and tell soldiers to go right or left? It is only because military leaders are surrounded by pomp, power, and crowds of sycophants who flatter authority by attributing to it qualities of genius it does not possess. The best generals I have known were, on the contrary, stupid or absent-minded men. Bagration was the best — Napoleon himself admitted it. And Napoleon himself! I remember his smug, self-satisfied face on the field of Austerlitz. Not only does a good commander not need any special qualities — on the contrary, he needs the absence of the highest and best human attributes: love, poetry, tenderness, and philosophic, questioning doubt. He should be narrow-minded, firmly convinced that what he is doing is enormously important (otherwise he will lack the necessary patience), and only then will he be a brave leader. God forbid that he should be humane, that he should love or feel pity, or think about what is just and unjust. It is no wonder that a theory of their 'genius' was invented for them long ago, because they hold power! The success of a military action depends not on them but on the man in the ranks who shouts 'We're lost!' or who shouts 'Hurrah!' And only in the ranks can one serve with the assurance of being truly useful."

A large group of generals gathered around him, and Count Rostopchin, who had come from Moscow, joined them. This distinguished company split into several groups, all discussing the advantages and disadvantages of the position, the state of the army, the suggested plans, the situation in Moscow, and military matters generally. Though they hadn't been summoned for that purpose and the gathering wasn't officially called one, they all felt this was essentially a council of war. The conversations all dealt with public affairs. If anyone shared or asked for personal news, it was done in a whisper, and they immediately returned to general matters. No jokes, laughter, or even smiles were seen among these men. They all clearly made an effort to rise to the gravity of the situation. And all these groups, while talking among themselves, tried to stay near the commander in chief — whose bench formed the center of the gathering — and to speak loudly enough for him to hear. The commander in chief listened and sometimes asked them to repeat their remarks, but did not join the conversations or express any opinion. After hearing what one group or another had to say, he generally turned away with a look of disappointment, as though they weren't discussing what he wanted to hear. Some debated the chosen position, criticizing not so much the position itself as the competence of those who'd chosen it. Others argued that a mistake had been made earlier — that a battle should have been fought two days ago. Still others talked about the Battle of Salamanca, described by Crosart, a newly arrived Frenchman in a Spanish uniform. (This Frenchman and one of the German princes serving with the Russian army were discussing the siege of Saragossa and whether Moscow could be defended in a similar way.) Count Rostopchin was telling a fourth group that he was prepared to die with the city militia under the capital's walls, but couldn't help regretting having been kept in the dark — had he known sooner, things would have been different. A fifth group, displaying the depth of their strategic thinking, discussed the direction the troops should now take. A sixth group was talking outright nonsense. Kutuzov's expression grew more and more troubled and gloomy. From all this talk he drew only one conclusion: that defending Moscow was physically impossible — in the fullest meaning of those words — so utterly impossible that if some senseless commander were to order a battle, the result would be chaos, not combat. It wouldn't happen because the commanders not only recognized the position as hopeless, but in their conversations were discussing only what would follow its inevitable abandonment. How could commanders lead their troops into battle on ground they considered impossible to hold? The lower-ranking officers and even the soldiers, who also think, considered the position hopeless as well, and therefore could not fight, fully convinced they would be defeated. If Bennigsen insisted on defending the position and others still debated it, the question was no longer important in itself — it merely served as a pretext for argument and intrigue. They left because for Russians there could be no question of whether things would go well or badly under French rule in Moscow. Being subject to French rule was out of the question — it would be the worst possible outcome. They left even before the Battle of Borodino, and even faster after it, despite Rostopchin's calls to defend Moscow, his announcement that he'd take the wonder-working icon of the Iberian Mother of God into battle, and his plans for hot-air balloons to destroy the French, and all the other nonsense he published in his broadsheets. They left without dwelling on the tremendous significance of a great city being handed over to destruction — for a great city of wooden buildings, once abandoned by its inhabitants, was certain to burn. Each left on his own account, and yet only because of their leaving was the momentous event accomplished that will always remain the greatest glory of the Russian people. The lady who, fearing she'd be stopped by Rostopchin's orders, had already moved to her Saratov estate in June with her Negroes and her women jesters, with a vague sense that she was not Bonaparte's servant, was truly carrying out the great work that saved Russia.
