And Napoleon, weeping in front of his Old Guard, gave up the throne and went into exile. Then the skillful statesmen and diplomats — Talleyrand above all, who managed to sit down in a particular chair before anyone else, and by doing so extended the borders of France — talked things over in Vienna, and by these conversations made whole nations happy or unhappy. Suddenly the diplomats and monarchs nearly fell out and were on the point of once again ordering their armies to kill one another, but just then Napoleon landed in France with a single battalion, and the French, who had been hating him, immediately submitted to him again, every one of them. But this enraged the Allied monarchs, and they went to fight the French once more. And they defeated the genius Napoleon and, suddenly declaring him a brigand after all, sent him off to the island of St. Helena. And the exile, cut off from the beloved France so dear to his heart, died a slow death on that rock, and left his great deeds to posterity. But in Europe a reaction set in, and the sovereigns all went back to oppressing their subjects."

It would be a mistake to think this is meant ironically — a caricature of historical writing. On the contrary, it is a fairly mild version of the contradictory answers, none of which actually meet the questions asked, given by all the historians, from the compilers of memoirs and the histories of individual states to the writers of general histories and the newest histories of the culture of that period.
The strangeness and absurdity of these answers comes from the fact that modern history, like a deaf man, answers questions nobody asked.

If the purpose of history is to describe the movement of humanity and of peoples, the first question — without an answer to which everything else remains incomprehensible — is: what is the force that moves peoples? To this, modern history laboriously answers either that Napoleon was a great genius, or that Louis XIV was very proud, or that certain writers wrote certain books.

All of that may well be true, and mankind is ready to agree with it, but it is not what was asked. All of it would be interesting if we accepted a divine power, grounded in itself, consistently steering its nations through the likes of Napoleons, Louis-es, and writers; but we do not accept such a power, and therefore, before talking about Napoleons, Louis-es, and authors, we need to be shown the connection between these men and the movement of the nations.
If some other force has taken the place of divine power, it needs to be explained what this new force actually consists of, because the whole interest of history lies precisely there.

History seems to take it for granted that this force is self-evident and known to everyone. But however much one might wish to treat it as known, anyone who reads a good number of historical works cannot help wondering whether this new force — understood so differently by the historians themselves — is really well understood by anybody at all.
What force moves the nations?

Historians who write biographies, or histories of a single nation, understand this force as a power built into heroes and rulers. In their telling, events happen purely by the will of a Napoleon, an Alexander, or whichever figure they are writing about. The answers this kind of historian gives to the question of what force makes events happen are satisfying only so long as a single historian is covering a single event. As soon as historians of different nationalities and different leanings start describing the same event, their answers immediately lose all meaning, because this force is understood by each of them not just differently, but often in flatly contradictory ways. One historian says an event was produced by Napoleon's power, another that it was produced by Alexander's, a third that it came from the power of some other person entirely. What's more, historians of this kind contradict one another even on the question of what a given person's authority was based on. Thiers, a Bonapartist, says Napoleon's power rested on his virtue and his genius. Lanfrey, a Republican, says it rested on his trickery and his deception of the people. So historians of this class, by tearing down each other's positions, tear down any understanding of the force that produces events, and give no answer at all to history's essential question.

Writers of universal history, who deal with all nations at once, seem to recognize how mistaken the specialist historians' view of the force producing events really is. They do not treat it as a power built into heroes and rulers, but as the resultant of many differently directed forces. In describing a war, or the subjugation of a people, a general historian looks for the cause of the event not in the power of one man, but in the interaction of the many people connected to that event.

On this view, the power of historical figures — presented as the product of many forces — can no longer, it would seem, be treated as a force that itself produces events. And yet in most cases the universal historians still use the idea of power as a force that produces events in its own right, and treat it as a cause. In their accounts, a historical figure is first the product of his era, his power merely the resultant of various forces — and then his power turns into a force producing events all by itself. Gervinus, Schlosser, and others, for instance, at one point prove that Napoleon was a product of the Revolution, of the ideas of 1789 and so on, and at another point flatly state that the campaign of 1812, and other things they disapprove of, were simply the product of Napoleon's misguided will, and that the very ideas of 1789 were stopped in their development by Napoleon's whim. The ideas of the Revolution and the general temper of the age produced Napoleon's power. But Napoleon's power suppressed the ideas of the Revolution and the general temper of the age.

This curious contradiction is not an accident. Not only does it turn up at every step, but the universal historians' accounts are made up, from end to end, of a chain of just such contradictions. It happens because once the universal historians enter the field of analysis, they stop halfway.

To find component forces equal to a composite or resultant force, the sum of the components must equal the resultant. The universal historians never observe this condition, and so, to explain the resultant forces, they are forced to bring in — alongside their insufficient components — some other, unexplained force acting on the outcome.

Specialist historians describing the campaign of 1813, or the restoration of the Bourbons, state plainly that these events were produced by Alexander's will. But the universal historian Gervinus, refuting this view of the specialist historians, tries to show that the campaign of 1813 and the restoration of the Bourbons came about because of other things besides Alexander's will — the activity of Stein, Metternich, Madame de Staël, Talleyrand, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others. The historian, in effect, breaks Alexander's power down into its components: Talleyrand, Chateaubriand, and the rest — but the sum of those components, that is, the interactions among Chateaubriand, Talleyrand, Madame de Staël, and the others, plainly does not add up to the resultant: the fact of millions of Frenchmen submitting to the Bourbons. The fact that Chateaubriand, Madame de Staël, and the others said certain things to one another only affected their own mutual relations, but does not account for the submission of millions. And so, to explain how the submission of millions of people resulted from these relations of theirs — that is, how component forces adding up to some quantity A produced a resultant a thousand times greater than A — the historian is forced to fall back once more on power, the very force he had just denied, and to treat it as the resultant of the forces — which means admitting an unexplained force acting on the outcome. And that is exactly what the universal historians do, and as a result they contradict not only the specialist historians but themselves.

Peasants, who have no clear idea of what causes rain, say, depending on whether they want rain or fine weather: "The wind has blown the clouds away," or, "The wind has brought up the clouds." In just the same way, the universal historians sometimes, when it suits them and fits their theory, say that power is the result of events, and sometimes, when they want to prove something else, say that power produces events.

A third class of historians — the so-called historians of culture — following the path laid down by the universal historians, who sometimes treat writers and society ladies as forces producing events, take that force to be something else again. They find it in what is called culture, in intellectual activity.

The historians of culture are entirely consistent with their forerunners, the writers of universal history: if historical events can be explained by the fact that certain people treated one another in such and such ways, why not explain them by the fact that certain people wrote certain books? Out of the immense number of signs that accompany every living phenomenon, these historians pick out the sign of intellectual activity and declare that this sign is the cause. But despite all their efforts to prove that the cause of events lies in intellectual activity, one can admit any connection at all between intellectual activity and the movement of peoples only with a considerable stretch, and one can never admit that intellectual activity controls people's actions — a view contradicted by facts such as the extremely cruel murders of the French Revolution, which grew out of the doctrine of the equality of man, or the extremely cruel wars and executions that grew out of the preaching of love.

But even granting as valid every one of the cleverly constructed arguments these histories are full of — even granting that nations are governed by some undefined force called an idea — history's essential question still goes unanswered, and to the old power of monarchs, and to the influence of advisers and other people brought in by the universal historians, a newer force is now added — the idea — whose connection to the masses still needs explaining. One can understand that Napoleon had power, and so events occurred; with some effort one can even accept that Napoleon, together with other influences, was the cause of an event; but how a book, Le Contrat Social, had the effect of making Frenchmen start drowning one another cannot be understood without an explanation of the causal chain linking this new force to the event.

Undoubtedly some relation exists among everyone who lives at the same time, and so it's possible to find some connection between men's intellectual activity and their historical movements, just as a connection can be found between the movements of humanity and commerce, handicraft, gardening, or anything else you like. But why intellectual activity in particular should be treated by the historians of culture as the cause, or as the expression, of the whole historical movement is hard to understand. Only the following considerations can have led historians to such a conclusion: (1) history is written by learned men, and so it is natural and gratifying for them to think that the activity of their own class provides the basis for the movement of all humanity — just as the same belief comes naturally and agreeably to merchants, farmers, and soldiers, (if they do not say so, it is simply because merchants and soldiers do not write history); and (2) spiritual activity, enlightenment, civilization, culture, ideas — these are all vague, indefinite notions, under whose banner it is very easy to use words with an even less definite meaning, which can therefore be worked into any theory whatsoever.

But setting aside the intrinsic worth of histories of this kind (which may perhaps even be useful to someone, for something), the histories of culture — which all general histories are increasingly coming to resemble — are revealing in this respect: after seriously and painstakingly examining various religious, philosophical, and political doctrines as the causes of events, the moment they have to describe an actual historical event, such as the campaign of 1812, they involuntarily describe it as the outcome of an exercise of power, and say plainly that it was the result of Napoleon's will. In saying this, the historians of culture unwittingly contradict themselves, and show that the new force they have invented does not actually account for what happens in history, and that history can only be explained by bringing in a power they apparently do not recognize.

A locomotive is moving. Someone asks, "What's making it move?" A peasant says the devil is moving it. Another man says the locomotive moves because its wheels go round. A third insists the cause of its movement lies in the smoke the wind is carrying off.

The peasant cannot be refuted. He has a complete explanation. To refute him, someone would have to prove to him that there is no devil, or another peasant would have to explain that it isn't the devil but a German who's moving the locomotive. Only then, through the contradiction between them, would they see that both are wrong. But the man who says the movement of the wheels is the cause refutes himself, because once he's begun to analyze, he ought to keep going and explain why the wheels turn — and until he has traced things back to the ultimate cause, the pressure of steam in the boiler, he has no right to stop looking. The man who explains the movement of the locomotive by the smoke being carried backward has noticed that the wheels don't really explain anything, and has simply grabbed the first sign that occurred to him and offered that instead.
The only idea that can explain the movement of the locomotive is that of a force commensurate with the movement we observe.
The only idea that can explain the movement of peoples is that of some force commensurate with the whole movement of the peoples.

Yet to supply this idea, various historians reach for forces of entirely different kinds, none of which is commensurate with the movement observed. Some see it as a force built directly into heroes, the way the peasant sees the devil in the locomotive; others see it as a force resulting from the interplay of several other forces, like the movement of the wheels; others again see it as an intellectual influence, like the smoke that is blown away.

So long as histories are written about individuals — whether Caesars, Alexanders, Luthers, or Voltaires — rather than histories of everyone, absolutely everyone, who took part in an event, it is simply impossible to describe the movement of humanity without the idea of a force compelling people to direct their activity toward some given end. And the only such idea known to historians is power.

This idea is the one handle by which the material of history, as it is presented today, can be picked up and handled at all, and anyone who breaks that handle off, as Buckle did, without finding some other way of dealing with the material, simply deprives himself of the one available way of handling it. The necessity of the idea of power for explaining historical events is best demonstrated by the universal historians and the historians of culture themselves, who profess to reject that idea and yet inevitably fall back on it at every step.

In dealing with humanity's great question, the science of history so far is like money in circulation — paper money and coin. Biographies and the histories of individual nations are like paper money. They can be used, they can circulate, and they can serve their purpose without doing anyone any harm, and even to real advantage, as long as no one asks what actually backs them. You only have to forget to ask how the will of heroes produces events, and histories like Thiers' will be interesting, instructive, and may even carry a certain poetry. But just as doubts about the real value of paper money arise either because it is easy to print and too much of it gets printed, or because people try to exchange it for gold, so too doubts about the real value of such histories arise either because too many of them get written, or because someone, in simple honesty, asks: by what force did Napoleon actually do this? — that is, wants to exchange the current paper money for the real gold of genuine understanding.

Writers of universal history and of the history of culture are like people who, recognizing the flaws of paper money, decide to replace it with coin made of some metal that doesn't have the specific weight of gold. It may make a nice jingling sound, but that's all it will do. Paper money can fool the ignorant, but nobody is fooled by tokens of base metal that have no real value beyond their jingle. Just as gold is gold only if it can be put to use and not merely exchanged, universal historians will only be worth something once they can answer history's essential question: what is power? The universal historians give contradictory answers to that question, while the historians of culture dodge it and answer something else entirely. And just as tokens of imitation gold can only be used among people who have agreed to accept them as gold, or among those who don't know what real gold is, so the universal historians and historians of culture, without answering humanity's essential question, serve as currency for purposes of their own — only in universities, and among the mass of readers with a taste for what they call "serious reading."

Having given up the ancients' idea that a nation's will is divinely subordinated to some chosen man, and that man's will in turn subordinated to God, history cannot take a single step without contradicting itself until it chooses one of two things: either return to the old belief in the direct intervention of God in human affairs, or arrive at a definite explanation of what is meant by that force which produces historical events and which we call "power."
A return to the first is impossible; the belief has been destroyed. And so it becomes essential to explain what power means.

Napoleon ordered an army raised and sent to war. We are so used to this idea, so accustomed to it, that the question of why six hundred thousand men went off to fight simply because Napoleon spoke certain words strikes us as senseless. He had the power, and so what he ordered was done.

This answer is entirely satisfactory if we believe the power was given to him by God. But the moment we stop believing that, it becomes essential to determine just what this power of one man over others actually is.

It cannot be the direct physical power of a strong man over a weak one — a domination based on applying or threatening physical force, like the strength of Hercules; nor can it rest on moral force, as some historians naively suppose when they say that the great figures of history are heroes, meaning men gifted with a special strength of soul and mind called genius. This power cannot rest on a predominance of moral strength, because — setting aside heroes like Napoleon, whose moral qualities are a matter of sharp disagreement — history shows us that neither a Louis XI nor a Metternich, both of whom ruled over millions of people, possessed any particular moral qualities; if anything, they were generally morally weaker than any of the millions they ruled.

If the source of power lies neither in the physical nor in the moral qualities of the one who holds it, then it must evidently be sought elsewhere — in the relation between the man who wields power and the people over whom he wields it.
And that is exactly how power is understood by the science of jurisprudence — that exchange bank of history, offering to trade history's understanding of power for real gold.
Power is the collective will of the people, transferred, through expressed or tacit consent, to their chosen rulers.

In the domain of jurisprudence, which consists of discussions about how a state and its power might be arranged if such an arrangement were possible at all, everything here is perfectly clear. But applied to history, this definition of power needs explaining.

The science of jurisprudence treats the state and power the way the ancients treated fire — as something that simply exists, absolutely. But for history, the state and power are merely phenomena, just as for modern physics fire is not an element but a phenomenon.

From this basic difference between the view held by history and the view held by jurisprudence, it follows that jurisprudence can tell us, in detail, how power ought in its opinion to be constituted, and what power is when treated as something fixed outside of time — but to history's questions about how power actually changes over time, it can give no answer at all.

If power is the collective will of the people transferred to their ruler, was Pugachev a representative of the people's will? If not, why was Napoleon I? Why was Napoleon III a criminal when he was captured at Boulogne, and why, later, were the people he himself arrested the criminals?

Do palace revolutions — in which sometimes only two or three people take part — transfer the people's will to a new ruler? In international relations, is the people's will also transferred to a conqueror? Was the will of the Confederation of the Rhine transferred to Napoleon in 1806? Was the will of the Russian people transferred to Napoleon in 1809, when our army, allied with the French, went to fight the Austrians?
To these questions three answers are possible:

Either (1) we assume that the will of the people is always transferred unconditionally to the ruler or rulers it has chosen, so that every emergence of a new power, every struggle against a power already appointed, must be regarded as a violation of the real power; or (2) we assume that the will of the people is transferred to rulers conditionally, under definite and known conditions, and show that every limitation on power, every conflict, even every destruction of power, results from the rulers' failure to observe the conditions under which their power was entrusted to them; or (3) we assume that the will of the people is delegated to rulers conditionally, but that the conditions are unknown and undefined, and that the rise of rival authorities, their struggles, and their falls, result simply from how well or badly the rulers fulfilled these unknown conditions under which the people's will passes from one person to another.
And these are the three ways historians actually do explain the relation between a people and its rulers.

Some historians — the biographical and specialist historians already mentioned — in their simplicity, fail to grasp the real question of what power means, and appear to assume that the collective will of the people is transferred unconditionally to historical figures; and so, in describing any single state, they treat that particular power as the one absolute, real power, and treat any force opposing it not as a power at all but as a violation of power — sheer violence.

Their theory, well suited to primitive and peaceful periods of history, runs into trouble when applied to complex and turbulent periods in the life of nations, during which several powers arise at once and struggle against one another — because a Legitimist historian will prove that the National Convention, the Directory, and Bonaparte were nothing but usurpers of the true power, while a Republican historian will prove that the Convention was the real power, and a Bonapartist that the Empire was, and that all the rest were violations of power. Since these explanations plainly contradict one another, they can satisfy no one but children.

Recognizing the falseness of this view of history, another group of historians say that power rests on a conditional delegation of the people's will to its rulers, and that historical leaders hold power only on condition of carrying out the program that the people's will has, by tacit agreement, prescribed for them. But what this program actually consists of, these historians do not say — or if they do, they keep contradicting one another.

Each historian, depending on his own view of what constitutes a nation's progress, looks for these conditions in the greatness, wealth, freedom, or enlightenment of the citizens of France or some other country. But setting aside the historians' disagreements over the nature of this program — even granting that some single, general program of these conditions exists — the facts of history almost always contradict the theory. If the conditions under which power is entrusted consist in the wealth, freedom, and enlightenment of the people, how is it that Louis XIV and Ivan the Terrible end their reigns peacefully, while Louis XVI and Charles I are executed by their own people? To this, historians answer that Louis XIV's conduct, though it went against the program, reacted on Louis XVI. But why did it not react on Louis XIV himself, or on Louis XV — why did it have to react precisely on Louis XVI? And what is the time limit on such delayed reactions? These questions have no answer, and can have none. Just as little does this view explain why, for several centuries, the collective will is never withdrawn from a given line of rulers and their heirs, and then suddenly, over the course of fifty years, passes to the Convention, to the Directory, to Napoleon, to Alexander, to Louis XVIII, to Napoleon again, to Charles X, to Louis Philippe, to a Republican government, and to Napoleon III. Trying to explain these rapid transfers of the people's will from one person to another — especially once international relations, conquests, and alliances are factored in — historians are forced to admit that some of these transfers are not genuine acts of delegation by the people's will at all, but accidents resulting from cunning, from mistakes, from craft, or from the weakness of some diplomat, ruler, or party leader. So that the greater part of the events of history — civil wars, revolutions, conquests — end up being presented by these very historians not as the outcome of free transfers of the people's will, but as the outcome of the misdirected will of one or a few individuals — that is, once again, as usurpations of power. And so these historians too end up seeing, and admitting, historical events that are exceptions to their own theory.

These historians resemble a botanist who, having noticed that some plants grow from seeds that produce two seed-leaves, insists that everything that grows must sprout in exactly that way, and that the palm, the mushroom, and even the oak — which grow into full maturity looking nothing like two leaves — are simply deviations from the theory.

Historians of the third class assume that the will of the people is transferred to historical figures conditionally, but that the conditions themselves are unknown to us. They say that historical figures hold power only because they carry out the will of the people that has been delegated to them.
But in that case, if the force that moves nations lies not in the historical leaders but in the nations themselves, what significance do those leaders have at all?

But then the question arises whether the entire activity of the leaders serves as an expression of the people's will, or only some part of it. If the whole of a leader's activity counts as an expression of the people's will, as some historians suppose, then every detail of court scandal found in the biographies of a Napoleon or a Catherine must also express the life of the nation — which is obvious nonsense. But if only some particular side of a historical leader's activity expresses the people's life, as other, so-called "philosophical" historians believe, then to determine which side of a leader's activity expresses the nation's life, we would first have to know what the nation's life actually consists of.

Faced with this difficulty, historians of this class devise some highly obscure, intangible, and general abstraction, broad enough to cover any conceivable occurrence, and declare this abstraction to be the goal of humanity's movement. The most common generalizations adopted by nearly all historians are: freedom, equality, enlightenment, progress, civilization, culture. Having set up some such generalization as the goal of humanity's movement, historians go on to study the men who left behind the greatest number of monuments — kings, ministers, generals, authors, reformers, popes, journalists — according to how far, in the historian's opinion, these people advanced or hindered that abstraction. But since it is nowhere proven that the goal of humanity actually consists in freedom, equality, enlightenment, or civilization, and since the connection between the people and the rulers and enlighteners of humanity rests only on the arbitrary assumption that the collective will of the people is always transferred to the men we happen to have noticed, it turns out that the activity of the millions who migrate, burn houses, abandon their fields, and destroy one another is never actually captured in the account of the activity of a dozen or so people who did none of that burning, farming, or killing.

History bears this out at every turn. Is the ferment among the peoples of the West at the end of the eighteenth century, and their surge eastward, explained by the activity of Louis XIV, XV, and XVI, their mistresses and their ministers, and by the lives of Napoleon, Rousseau, Diderot, Beaumarchais, and the rest?
Is the movement of the Russian people eastward, toward Kazan and Siberia, captured in the details of Ivan the Terrible's disturbed character, or in his correspondence with Kurbsky?

Is the movement of the peoples at the time of the Crusades explained by the lives and activities of the Godfreys and the Louis-es and their ladies? For us, that movement of peoples from west to east, leaderless, made up of a crowd of wanderers, and with Peter the Hermit among them, remains incomprehensible. And still more incomprehensible is the way that movement stopped once a rational and sacred goal for the Crusade — the liberation of Jerusalem — had been clearly spelled out by the historical leaders. Popes, kings, and knights urged the peoples on to free the Holy Land; but the people did not go, because the unknown cause that had earlier driven them to go no longer existed. The history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers plainly cannot cover the life of the peoples. And the history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers has remained just that — the history of the Godfreys and the Minnesingers — while the history of the life of the peoples and their impulses has remained unknown.
Still less does the history of authors and reformers explain the life of the peoples to us.

The history of culture explains to us the impulses and living conditions and thoughts of a writer or a reformer. We learn that Luther had a hot temper and said such and such things; we learn that Rousseau was suspicious of everyone and wrote such and such books; but we do not learn why, after the Reformation, whole peoples massacred one another, or why, during the French Revolution, they went on guillotining each other.
If we combine both these kinds of history, as the newest historians do, we end up with a history of monarchs and writers — but not a history of the life of the peoples.

The life of nations is not contained in the lives of a handful of men, because no connection between those men and the nations has ever been found. The theory that this connection rests on the transfer of the people's collective will to certain historical figures is a hypothesis unsupported by the experience of history.

The theory of the transfer of the people's collective will to historical figures may explain a great deal within the domain of jurisprudence, and may even be essential for its purposes; but applied to history, the moment revolutions, conquests, or civil wars occur — that is, the moment history actually begins — that theory explains nothing at all.
The theory looks irrefutable precisely because the act of transferring the people's will can never be verified, since it never took place.
Whatever happens, and whoever ends up at the head of affairs, the theory can always claim that this person took the lead because the collective will was transferred to him.

The answers this theory gives to historical questions resemble the answers of a man who, watching a herd of cattle move, pays no attention to the varying quality of pasture in different parts of the field, or to the herdsman driving them, and instead credits the direction the herd takes to whichever animal happens to be walking in front.

"The herd is heading that way because the animal in front is leading it, and the collective will of all the other animals has been vested in that leader." This is what historians of the first class say — those who assume the people's will is transferred unconditionally.

"If the animals leading the herd keep changing, that's because the collective will of all the animals is transferred from one leader to another, depending on whether the animal is or isn't leading them in the direction the whole herd has chosen." That is the answer given by historians who assume that the collective will of the people is delegated to rulers under conditions they take to be known. (With this method of observation, the observer, swayed by whichever direction he himself prefers, often ends up calling those animals leaders who, because the herd has changed direction, are no longer in front at all, but off to one side, or even at the back.)

"If the animals in front keep changing and the whole herd's direction keeps shifting, that's because, in order to follow a given direction, the animals transfer their will to whichever animals have caught our attention, and so to study the movements of the herd we have to watch the movements of all the prominent animals on every side of it." So say the third class of historians, who treat every historical figure, from monarchs to journalists, as the expression of their age.
The theory of the transfer of the people's will to historical figures is nothing but a paraphrase — a restatement of the question in different words.

What causes historical events? Power. What is power? Power is the collective will of the people transferred to one person. Under what condition is the people's will delegated to one person? On condition that this person expresses the will of the whole people. That is: power is power — in other words, power is a word whose meaning we do not understand.

If the realm of human knowledge were limited to abstract reasoning, then, having subjected the jurists' explanation of "power" to criticism, mankind would conclude that power is merely a word with no real existence behind it. But to understand phenomena, man has, besides abstract reasoning, experience, by which he tests his reasoning. And experience tells us that power is not merely a word, but a phenomenon that actually exists.

Not to mention that no description of the collective activity of men can do without the idea of power at all, the existence of power is proven both by history and by observing events happening around us now.

Whenever an event occurs, a man appears, or several men appear, by whose will the event seems to have taken place. Napoleon III issues a decree, and the French go to Mexico. The King of Prussia and Bismarck issue decrees, and an army enters Bohemia. Napoleon I issues a decree, and an army enters Russia. Alexander I gives a command, and the French submit to the Bourbons. Experience shows us that, whatever the event, it is always tied to the will of one or several men who decreed it.

Historians, following the old habit of acknowledging divine intervention in human affairs, want to see the cause of events in the expressed will of someone who holds power — but that assumption is confirmed neither by reason nor by experience.

On one hand, reflection shows that the expression of a man's will — his words — is only part of the general activity expressed in an event, as for example in a war or a revolution, and so, without assuming some incomprehensible, supernatural force — a miracle — one cannot accept that words alone could be the immediate cause of the movements of millions of men. On the other hand, even granting that words could be the cause of events, history shows that the expressed will of historical figures very often produces no effect at all — that their commands are frequently not carried out, and sometimes the exact opposite of what they order happens instead.
Without admitting divine intervention in human affairs, we cannot treat "power" as the cause of events.
Power, seen from the standpoint of experience, is simply the relationship that exists between the expression of someone's will and the carrying out of that will by others.
To explain the conditions of that relationship, we must first establish a conception of the expression of will as it applies to man, not to God.

If God issues a command, expresses His will, as ancient history tells us, then the expression of that will is independent of time and caused by nothing, since the Divine is not subject to events. But when we speak of commands that express the will of men acting in time and in relation to one another, then, to explain the connection between commands and events, we must restore two things: (1) the condition underlying everything that happens — the continuity of movement in time, both of the events themselves and of the person giving the command — and (2) the inevitable connection between the person giving the command and those who carry it out.

Only the expression of God's will, independent of time, can apply to a whole chain of events unfolding over years or centuries, and only God, independent of everything, can by His will alone determine the direction of humanity's movement; but man acts in time, and takes part himself in what happens.

Restoring the first condition we left out — that of time — we see that no command can be carried out without some earlier order having already been given that makes carrying out the later command possible.

No command ever appears out of nowhere, and no single command covers a whole chain of events on its own; each command follows from another, and never refers to a whole series of events, only to one moment of an event.

When, for instance, we say Napoleon ordered his armies to go to war, we are compressing into one simultaneous statement a whole series of consecutive commands, each dependent on the last. Napoleon could not have ordered, and never did order, an invasion of Russia as a single act. Today he ordered such and such dispatches written to Vienna, to Berlin, to Petersburg; tomorrow such and such decrees and orders to the army, the navy, the commissariat, and so on and so on — millions of commands, forming a whole series that corresponded to the series of events which brought the French armies into Russia.

If, throughout his reign, Napoleon issued commands about invading England, and spent more time and effort on that scheme than on anything else, and yet, across his entire reign, never once actually attempted to carry it out, while he did undertake an expedition into Russia, a country with which he repeatedly said he thought it desirable to remain allied — that happened because his commands did not correspond to the actual course of events in the first case, but did correspond to it in the second.

For an order to be reliably carried out, it is necessary that a man order something that can actually be carried out. But knowing in advance what can and cannot be carried out is impossible — not just in a case like Napoleon's invasion of Russia, in which millions of people took part, but even in the simplest event, since in either case a million obstacles can arise to prevent it. Every order that is carried out is always just one out of an immense number that go uncarried out. All the impossible orders, the ones inconsistent with the course of events, simply go uncarried out. Only the possible ones link up with a consecutive series of commands matching a series of events, and get carried out.

Our mistaken idea that an event is caused by the command that precedes it comes from the fact that once the event has happened, out of thousands of commands only the handful consistent with that event were actually carried out, and we forget all about the rest, which went uncarried out simply because they couldn't be. Beyond that, the main source of our error here is that in historical accounts, a whole series of countless, varied, petty events — like all the ones that led the French armies into Russia — gets generalized into a single event, matching the result that series of events produced, and to match this generalization, the whole series of commands also gets generalized into a single expression of will.

We say that Napoleon wanted to invade Russia, and invaded it. In reality, nowhere in the whole of Napoleon's activity do we find anything resembling a single expression of that wish; instead we find a long series of orders, or expressions of his will, pointed in all sorts of different and indefinite directions. Out of a long series of Napoleon's orders that were never carried out, one series — the one for the campaign of 1812 — was carried out, not because those particular orders were any different from the rest that went uncarried out, but because they happened to coincide with the actual course of events that led the French army into Russia. It is exactly as in stencil work: this or that figure comes out not because the paint was applied from this side or that, but because it was applied everywhere, all over the figure cut into the stencil.
So when we examine the relation in time between commands and events, we find that a command can never be the cause of an event, but that a definite kind of dependence does exist between the two.

To understand what this dependence consists of, we need to restore another condition we left out — one that applies to every command that comes not from God but from a man: namely, that the man giving the command himself takes part in the event.
This relation between the one who commands and those he commands is exactly what we call power. This relation consists of the following.

For joint action, people always come together in certain arrangements in which, whatever differences there may be in the goals set for the joint action, the relation among the people taking part is always the same.

When people come together in these arrangements, they always settle into relations such that the larger number take the more direct part, and the smaller number the less direct part, in the collective action they have joined together to perform.
Of all the arrangements in which people join together for collective action, one of the most striking and clear-cut examples is an army.

Every army is made up of the lowest ranks — the rank and file — of whom there are always the greatest number; then the next rank up — corporals and noncommissioned officers — of whom there are fewer; then still-higher officers, of whom there are fewer still; and so on, up to the highest military command, which is concentrated in a single person.

A military organization can quite accurately be compared to a cone, whose base, with the widest diameter, consists of the rank and file; the next, smaller section of the cone consists of the next grades up in the army; and so on up to the apex, whose point represents the commander in chief.

The soldiers, of whom there are the most, make up the lower section of the cone, its base. The soldier himself does the stabbing, the hacking, the burning, the pillaging, and always receives his orders for these actions from men above him; he himself never gives an order. The noncommissioned officers, of whom there are fewer, carry out the action itself less often than the soldiers do, but they already give commands. An officer acts directly even less often, but commands still more. A general does nothing but command the troops, point out the objective, and almost never uses a weapon himself. The commander in chief never takes any direct part in the action itself, but only issues general orders about the movement of the whole mass of troops. The same kind of relation among people shows up in every combination of men formed for a common activity — in farming, in trade, in every kind of administration.

And so, without going through every adjoining layer of the cone, every rank in the army, or every position in any administrative or public undertaking from the lowest to the highest, we can see a law: that people, in order to act together, combine in relations such that the more directly they take part in carrying out the action, the less they command and the more numerous they are, while the less direct their part in the action itself, the more they command and the fewer of them there are — rising this way from the lowest ranks up to the man at the very top, who takes the least direct part in the action and directs his activity almost entirely to commanding.
This relation between those who command and those who are commanded is what makes up the essence of the idea we call power.

Having restored the condition of time under which all events occur, we find that a command is carried out only when it corresponds to a matching series of events. Having restored the essential condition of the relation between those who command and those who carry out, we find that, by the very nature of things, those who command take the smallest part in the action itself, and that their activity is directed almost entirely to commanding.

When an event is taking place, people voice their opinions and wishes about it, and since the event results from the collective activity of many people, one of the opinions or wishes expressed is bound to come true, at least approximately. When one of these expressed opinions comes true, it gets linked to the event as though it were a command that preceded it.

Some men are hauling a log. Each of them says how and where he thinks it should be hauled. They haul the log away, and it turns out to have been done the way one of them said. He gave the order. There we have command and power in their most basic form. The man who did the most physical work could hardly think much about what he was doing, or plan out or command what the joint effort would produce; while the man who did more commanding would obviously work less with his hands, given how much more talking he was doing.

When a larger group of people direct their activity toward a shared goal, there is a still sharper split between those whose activity goes toward directing and commanding and who therefore take less part in the direct work.

When a man works alone, he always has a certain set of reflections which, as it seems to him, guided his past activity, justify his present activity, and steer his plans for the future. A group of people does exactly the same thing, letting those who don't take a direct part in the activity work out considerations, justifications, and guesses about their collective activity.

For reasons known or unknown to us, the French began drowning and killing one another. And to match the event, its justification appeared: the belief that this was necessary for the welfare of France, for liberty, for equality. People stopped killing one another, and this event too came with its justification: the necessity of centralizing power, of resisting Europe, and so on. Men marched from west to east killing their fellow men, and the event came wrapped in phrases about the glory of France, the baseness of England, and so on. History shows us that these justifications make no sense at all and contradict one another — as when killing a man is justified by an appeal to his rights, and the killing of millions in Russia is justified by the need to humiliate England. But in their own day, these justifications carry a very real and necessary meaning.

These justifications free the people who produce events from moral responsibility. These temporary goals are like the broom fixed to the front of a locomotive to clear snow off the rails ahead: they clear men's moral responsibility out of their path.

Without such justification, there would be no answer at all to the simplest question that comes up when examining any historical event: how is it that millions of men commit collective crimes — wage war, commit murder, and so on?

Given the complicated forms of political and social life in Europe today, can any event be imagined that is not prescribed, decreed, or ordered by monarchs, ministers, parliaments, or newspapers? Is there any collective action that cannot find its justification in political unity, in patriotism, in the balance of power, or in civilization? So that every event that occurs inevitably coincides with some expressed wish, and, once it has found its justification, presents itself as the result of the will of one man, or of several men.
Whichever direction a ship is moving, the wake it cuts will always be visible just ahead of it. To the people on board, the movement of that wake will seem like the only perceptible motion there is.

Only by watching, moment by moment, the movement of that wake, and comparing it with the movement of the ship, do we convince ourselves that every bit of it is caused by the ship moving forward, and that we were misled because we ourselves were moving without noticing it.

We see the same thing if we watch, moment by moment, the movement of historical figures — that is, if we restore the necessary condition of everything that happens, the continuity of movement in time — and if we never lose sight of the essential connection between historical figures and the masses.

When the ship moves in one direction, there is one and the same wave ahead of it; when it turns often, the wave ahead of it turns often too. But wherever it turns, there will always be a wave anticipating its movement.

Whatever happens, it always looks as though that very event had been foreseen and decreed. Wherever the ship goes, the rush of water ahead of it — which neither steers it nor speeds it up — foams out in front, and from a distance seems not merely to move on its own but to govern the ship's movement too.

By examining only those expressions of the will of historical figures which, as commands, could be linked to events, historians have assumed that events depended on those commands. But by examining the events themselves, and the connection historical figures actually had to the people, we have found that they, and their orders, were dependent on events instead. The undeniable proof of this conclusion is that, no matter how many commands are issued, the event does not happen unless other causes exist for it — but as soon as an event does happen, whatever it may be, then, out of all the continually expressed wishes of different people, some will always be found which, by their meaning and their timing, can be linked to the event as commands.
Arriving at this conclusion, we can now answer directly and positively history's two essential questions:
(2) What force produces the movement of the nations?

(1) Power is the relation of a given person to other individuals, in which the more this person expresses opinions, predictions, and justifications for the collective action being carried out, the less he actually takes part in that action.

(2) The movement of nations is caused not by power, nor by intellectual activity, nor even by some combination of the two, as historians have supposed, but by the activity of all the people who take part in the events, and who always combine in such a way that those who take the largest direct share in an event bear the least responsibility for it, and vice versa.

Morally, it looks as though the person wielding power causes the event; physically, it is those who submit to that power who cause it. But since moral activity is inconceivable apart from physical activity, the cause of the event lies neither in the one nor the other, but in the union of the two.
Or, put another way, the very idea of a "cause" does not apply to the phenomena we are examining here.

In the last analysis, we arrive at the circle of infinity — that final boundary which human reason, in every field of thought, reaches whenever it is not merely toying with its subject. Electricity produces heat; heat produces electricity. Atoms attract one another; atoms repel one another.

Speaking of the interaction between heat and electricity, or between atoms, we cannot say why it happens; we simply say that it is so, because it is inconceivable otherwise, because it has to be so, and call it a law. The same applies to historical events. Why wars and revolutions happen, we do not know. We only know that to produce one action or the other, people combine into a certain formation in which they all take part, and we say this is so because it cannot be thought of otherwise — in other words, that it is a law.

If history dealt only with external phenomena, establishing this simple, obvious law would be enough, and we could consider the argument finished. But the law of history concerns man. A particle of matter cannot tell us that it doesn't feel the pull of attraction or repulsion and that the law is false — but man, who is the subject of history, says plainly: I am free, and therefore not subject to the law.
The problem of man's free will, even when it goes unspoken, makes itself felt at every step of history.

Every historian who has thought seriously about the subject has run up against this question, whether he wanted to or not. All the contradictions and obscurities in history, and the false path historical science has followed, come down to nothing but the failure to solve that question.
If every man's will were free — if each man could act however he pleased — then all of history would be nothing but a series of disconnected incidents.

If, over the course of a thousand years, even one man in a million could act freely, that is, exactly as he chose, then it is obvious that a single free act by that one man, in violation of the laws governing human action, would destroy the very possibility of there being any laws at all for the whole of humanity.
If there is even one law governing the actions of men, free will cannot exist, because then a man's will is subject to that law.

In this contradiction lies the problem of free will, which since the most ancient times has occupied the best human minds, and since the most ancient times has been presented in the full weight of its significance.

The problem is this: if we consider man as an object of observation, from whatever standpoint — theological, historical, ethical, or philosophical — we find a general law of necessity to which he, like everything that exists, is subject. But if we look at him from within, as something we are directly conscious of, we feel ourselves to be free.
This consciousness is a source of self-knowledge entirely separate from, and independent of, reason. Through reason, man observes himself; but only through consciousness does he know himself.
Apart from consciousness of self, no observation and no use of reason is even conceivable.

To understand, to observe, to draw conclusions, a man must first of all be conscious of himself as a living being. A man is only conscious of himself as living through the fact that he wills — that is, that he is conscious of his own volition. But his will, which forms the very essence of his life, he can only recognize, and cannot help recognizing, as free.

If, watching himself, a man sees that his will is always steered by one and the same law — whether he is observing his need to eat, or to use his mind, or anything else — he can only recognize this unvarying direction of his will as a limitation on it. If it weren't free, it couldn't be limited. A man's will seems limited to him only because he is never conscious of it except as free.
You say: I am not free. But I have lifted my hand and let it fall. Everyone understands that this illogical answer is an irrefutable demonstration of freedom.
That answer expresses a consciousness that is not subject to reason.

If the consciousness of freedom were not a separate and independent source of self-consciousness, it would be subject to reasoning and to experience — but in fact no such subjection exists, and none is even conceivable.

A whole series of experiments and arguments proves to every man that, as an object of observation, he is subject to certain laws, and man submits to them, and never resists the laws of gravity or of solidity once he has learned them. But that same series of experiments and arguments proves to him that the complete freedom he is conscious of in himself is impossible, that his every action depends on his makeup, his character, and the motives acting on him — and yet man never submits to the conclusions of these experiments and arguments. Having learned from experiment and argument that a stone falls downward, a man believes this without question, and always expects the law he has learned to hold.
But learning, with equal certainty, that his will is subject to laws, he does not, and cannot, believe it.

However often experiment and reasoning show a man that under the same conditions, with the same character, he will do the same thing as before, when, under those same conditions and with that same character, he approaches for the thousandth time an action that always ends the same way, he feels just as certain as he did before the experiment that he can act however he pleases. Every man, savage or sage, however irrefutably reason and experiment may prove to him that it is impossible to imagine two different courses of action under exactly the same conditions, feels that without this irrational notion — which is the very essence of freedom — he cannot make sense of life. He feels that however impossible it may be, it must be so, because without this idea of freedom he would not only be unable to understand life, he would be unable to live for even a single moment.

He could not live, because every one of man's efforts, every impulse toward life, is nothing but an effort to increase freedom. Wealth and poverty, fame and obscurity, power and subordination, strength and weakness, health and sickness, culture and ignorance, work and leisure, having enough and going hungry, virtue and vice — these are all just greater or lesser degrees of freedom.
A man with no freedom at all cannot be conceived of except as a man deprived of life.

If the idea of freedom looks, to reason, like a senseless contradiction — like the possibility of performing two actions at the very same instant, or an effect without a cause — that only proves that consciousness is not subject to reason.

This unshakeable, irrefutable consciousness of freedom, which no experiment or argument can touch, which every thinker has recognized and every person without exception has felt, this consciousness without which no conception of man is even possible, makes up the other side of the question.
Man is the creation of an all-powerful, all-good, all-seeing God. What is sin — the idea that arises from man's consciousness of his own freedom? That is a question for theology.

The actions of men are subject to general, unchanging laws expressed in statistics. What is man's responsibility to society — the idea that follows from the idea of freedom? That is a question for jurisprudence.

A man's actions arise from his innate character and the motives acting on him. What is conscience, and the perception of right and wrong in actions, which follows from the consciousness of freedom? That is a question for ethics.

Man, seen in connection with the general life of humanity, appears subject to the laws that determine that life. But the same man, apart from that connection, appears to be free. How should the past life of nations, and of humanity, be regarded — as the result of man's free activity, or as the result of his constrained activity? That is a question for history.

Only in our own self-satisfied age of popularized knowledge — thanks to that most powerful engine of ignorance, the mass circulation of printed matter — has the question of free will been reduced to a level on which the question itself can no longer even exist. In our time, the majority of so-called advanced people — that is, the crowd of ignoramuses — have taken the work of naturalists, who deal with only one side of the question, for a solution to the whole problem.

They say, and write, and print, that the soul and free will do not exist, because man's life is expressed in muscular movements, and muscular movements are conditioned by the activity of the nerves; that the soul and free will do not exist because, at some unknown point in time, we descended from apes. They say this without the least suspicion that this same law of necessity, which they are now trying so eagerly to prove through physiology and comparative zoology, was not merely acknowledged, but never once denied, by every religion and every thinker thousands of years ago. They fail to see that the role of the natural sciences here is simply to serve as an instrument for illuminating one side of the question. The fact that, from the standpoint of observation, reason and will are merely secretions of the brain, and that man, following the general law, may have developed from lower animals at some unknown point in time, only restates from a new angle a truth admitted thousands of years ago by every religious and philosophical system: that from the standpoint of reason, man is subject to the law of necessity. But it does not advance the solution of the question by a hair's breadth, because the question has another side, the opposite side, grounded in the consciousness of freedom.

If men descended from apes at some unknown point in time, that is just as comprehensible as their having been made from a handful of earth at some fixed point in time — in the first case the unknown quantity is the time, in the second it is the origin — and the question of how man's consciousness of freedom can be reconciled with the law of necessity to which he is subject cannot be solved by comparative physiology and zoology, because in a frog, a rabbit, or an ape we can observe only muscular and nervous activity, but in man we observe consciousness as well as muscular and nervous activity.

The naturalists, and their followers, who think they can settle this question, are like plasterers assigned to plaster one side of a church wall who, taking advantage of the head foreman's absence, get carried away and plaster right over the windows, the icons, the woodwork, and the still-unbuttressed walls — and are delighted that, from a plasterer's point of view, everything now looks so smooth and even.

In solving the question of free will versus inevitability, history has one advantage over the other branches of knowledge that deal with the question: for history, the question does not concern the essence of man's free will as such, but only its manifestation in the past, under specific conditions.
With respect to this question, history stands to the other sciences the way experimental science stands to abstract science.

And so for history, the insoluble mystery presented by the incompatibility of free will and inevitability, which exists for theology, ethics, and philosophy, does not exist in the same way. History looks at a picture of man's life in which the union of these two contradictions has already taken place.

In actual life, every historical event, every human action, is understood very clearly and definitely, without any sense of contradiction, even though every event presents itself as partly free and partly compelled.

To resolve the question of how freedom and necessity combine, and what constitutes the essence of these two ideas, the philosophy of history can and should take the opposite path from the other sciences. Instead of first defining the ideas of freedom and inevitability on their own, and then sorting the phenomena of life under those definitions, history should derive its definition of freedom and inevitability from the immense quantity of phenomena it has before it — phenomena that always appear to depend on these two elements.
Whatever picture we consider of the activity of many men, or of a single individual, we always take it to be the result partly of man's free will and partly of the law of inevitability.

Whether we're talking about the migrations of peoples and the incursions of barbarians, or the decrees of Napoleon III, or someone's choice, an hour ago, of one direction over several possible ones for a walk, we are not conscious of any contradiction. The degree of freedom and the degree of inevitability governing these people's actions seem clearly defined to us.

Our sense of how much freedom is involved often shifts depending on the point of view from which we look at the event, but every human action appears to us as some combination of freedom and inevitability. In every action we examine, we see a certain measure of freedom and a certain measure of inevitability. And always, the more freedom we see in an action, the less inevitability we perceive, and the more inevitability, the less freedom.
The proportion of freedom to inevitability shrinks and grows depending on the point of view from which we regard the action, but the relation between them is always an inverse one.

A drowning man who grabs onto someone else and pulls him under; a hungry mother, worn out from feeding her baby, who steals food; a soldier trained to obey discipline who, on duty, kills a defenseless man at the word of command — all of these seem less guilty, that is, less free and more subject to the law of necessity, to someone who knows the circumstances these people were in, and more free to someone who does not know that the man was himself drowning, that the mother was starving, that the soldier was standing in the ranks under orders, and so on. In the same way, a man who committed a murder twenty years ago and has since lived peacefully and harmlessly in society seems less guilty, and his action more the product of the law of inevitability, to someone considering it twenty years later than to someone who examined it the day after it happened. And in just the same way, every action of an insane man, a drunk man, or a man in a state of high excitement seems less free and more inevitable to someone who knows the mental state of the person who did it, and seems more free and less inevitable to someone who doesn't know it. In every one of these cases, our sense of freedom grows or shrinks, and our sense of compulsion shrinks or grows correspondingly, depending on the point of view from which we look at the action. So that the greater our sense of necessity, the smaller our sense of freedom, and the other way around.
Religion, the common sense of mankind, the science of jurisprudence, and history itself all understand this relation between necessity and freedom in the same way.
Every single case in which our sense of freedom and necessity increases or decreases depends on three considerations:
(1) The relation of the man who commits the act to the external world.
(2) His relation to time.
(3) His relation to the causes that led to the action.

The first consideration is how clearly we perceive the man's relation to the external world, and how clearly we understand the particular position he occupies among everything that coexists with him. This is what makes it obvious that a drowning man is less free and more subject to necessity than a man standing on dry land, and why the actions of a man tightly bound up with others in a densely populated area, or bound by family, professional, or business obligations, seem clearly less free and more subject to necessity than the actions of a man living alone, in isolation.

If we consider a man in isolation, apart from his relation to everything around him, every one of his actions seems free to us. But the moment we see his relation to anything around him — his connection to anything at all, a person speaking to him, a book he is reading, the work he is engaged in, even the air he breathes or the light falling on the things around him — we see that each of these circumstances influences him and controls at least some part of his activity. And the more of these influences we perceive, the more our sense of his freedom shrinks, and the more our sense of the necessity weighing on him grows.

The second consideration is how clear or unclear the man's relation to time is, and how clearly we perceive the place his action occupies in time. This is the reason the fall of the first man, which resulted in the whole human race, seems clearly less free than a man's marrying today. It's the reason the life and activity of people who lived centuries ago, connected to me only through time, cannot seem to me as free as the life of a contemporary, whose consequences are still unknown to me.
The degree of our sense of freedom or inevitability depends, in this respect, on how much or how little time has passed between the performance of the action and our judgment of it.

If I examine an act I performed a moment ago, in roughly the same circumstances I am in now, the action seems to me undoubtedly free. But if I examine an act performed a month ago, now that I am in different circumstances, I cannot help recognizing that if that act had not been committed, much that came from it — good, pleasant, even essential — would not have happened. If I think back on an action still further in the past, ten years ago or more, the consequences of my action become even plainer to me, and I find it hard to imagine what would have happened had I not performed it. The further back I go in memory — or, which comes to the same thing, the further forward I go in judgment — the more doubtful my belief in the freedom of my own action becomes.

In history we find a very similar progression of conviction concerning the part free will plays in the general affairs of humanity. A contemporary event seems to us, without question, the doing of everyone known to be involved in it; but with a more distant event, we already see its inevitable results, results that rule out any possibility of things having gone otherwise. And the further back we go in examining events, the less arbitrary they appear.

The Austro-Prussian war seems to us, without doubt, the result of Bismarck's cunning maneuvering, and so on. The Napoleonic wars still seem to us, though already less certainly, the result of their heroes' will. But in the Crusades, we already see an event occupying a definite place in history, one without which we cannot imagine the subsequent history of Europe, even though to the chroniclers of the Crusades that event appeared to be simply the result of certain people's will. As for the migration of the peoples, it does not occur to anyone today to suppose that the remaking of the European world depended on Attila's whim. The further back in history the object of our observation lies, the more doubtful the free will of those involved in the event becomes, and the more evident the law of inevitability.

The third consideration is the degree to which we grasp that endless chain of causation, which reason inevitably demands, in which every phenomenon we understand — and therefore every one of man's actions — must have its own definite place, as the result of what came before and the cause of what will follow.

The better we know the physiological, psychological, and historical laws that observation has established, laws by which man is governed, and the more accurately we perceive the physiological, psychological, and historical causes of an action, and the simpler the action we are observing, and the less complex the character and mind of the person involved, the more subject to inevitability, and the less free, our own actions and those of others appear to us.

When we don't understand the cause of an action at all — whether it's a crime, a good deed, or even something simply neither one nor the other — we credit it with a greater degree of freedom. In the case of a crime, we demand punishment for it most urgently of all; in the case of a virtuous act, we rate its merit most highly. In a neutral case, we see in it more individuality, more originality, more independence. But if even one of the countless causes of the act becomes known to us, we recognize a certain element of necessity in it, and we grow less insistent on punishing the crime, or praising the virtuous act, or crediting the seemingly original action with real freedom. That a criminal was raised among criminals lessens his guilt in our eyes. The self-sacrifice of a father or a mother, or self-sacrifice that comes with some hope of reward, is easier to understand than self-sacrifice with no reward at all, and so it strikes us as less deserving of sympathy and less the result of free will. The founder of a sect, or of a political party, or an inventor, impresses us less once we know how, or by what means, the ground was prepared for his work. If we have a large stock of examples before us, if our attention is constantly bent on tracing the connection between cause and effect in people's actions, then the more correctly we trace effects back to their causes, the more compelled and the less free their actions appear to us. If we examined simple actions, and had a vast number of such actions under observation, our sense of their inevitability would be even greater still. The dishonest conduct of the son of a dishonest father, the misbehavior of a woman who has fallen in with bad company, a drunkard's relapse into drinking, and so on, are all actions that seem less free to us the better we understand their cause. If the man whose actions we are considering stands on a very low level of mental development — a child, a madman, a simpleton — then, knowing the causes of the act and the simplicity of the character and intelligence involved, we see so large an element of necessity, and so little free will, that as soon as we know the cause behind the action, we can predict the result.

These three considerations alone are the basis for the idea of diminished responsibility for crimes, and for the extenuating circumstances recognized by every legal code. Responsibility appears greater or smaller depending on how much or how little we know about the circumstances the person being judged was placed in, on how much or how little time has passed between the act and its investigation, and on how much or how little we understand the causes that led to the action.

In this way, our conception of free will and inevitability gradually shrinks or grows depending on how closely or loosely we connect a man to the external world, how remote or recent the time is, and how dependent or independent the causes are, in relation to which we consider a man's life.

So that if we examine a man whose connection to the external world is well known, where a great deal of time separates the action from our examination of it, and where the causes of the action are most accessible to us, we arrive at the conception of a maximum of inevitability and a minimum of free will. If we examine a man who depends little on external conditions, whose action took place very recently, and whose causes lie beyond our knowledge, we arrive at the conception of a minimum of inevitability and a maximum of freedom.

In neither case — however much we shift our point of view, however clearly or however obscurely we make out the connection between the man and the external world, however long or short the interval of time, however comprehensible or incomprehensible the causes of the action — can we ever arrive at a conception of either complete freedom or complete necessity.

(1) No matter to what degree we imagine a man exempt from the influence of the external world, we never arrive at a conception of freedom in space. Every human action is inevitably conditioned by what surrounds him and by his own body. I raise my arm and let it fall. My action seems free to me; but when I ask myself whether I could have raised it in every possible direction, I see that I raised it in the direction where there was the least obstruction to the action, either from the things around me or from the way my own body is built. Out of every possible direction, I chose the one with the fewest obstacles. For my action to be free, it would have had to meet no obstacle at all. To imagine a man as free, we would have to imagine him outside of space — which is plainly impossible.

(2) No matter how closely we bring the moment of judgment up against the moment of the deed, we never arrive at a conception of freedom in time. If I examine an action carried out a second ago, I still have to recognize it as unfree, because it is irrevocably tied to the instant at which it was performed. Can I lift my arm? I lift it — but then I ask myself: could I have refrained from lifting it at that moment, the one that has already passed? To convince myself, I don't lift it the next moment. But in not lifting it, I am not now refraining from doing so at that first moment when I asked the question. Time has gone by, time I could not hold back; the arm I lifted then is not the same arm I am now refraining from lifting, nor is the air I lifted it in the same air that surrounds me now. The moment in which that first movement happened is irrevocable, and in that moment I could make only one movement, and whatever movement I made was the only one possible. That I did not lift my arm a moment later proves nothing about whether I could have refrained from lifting it then. And since at that single moment of time I could make only one movement, it could not have been any other. To imagine it as free, we would have to imagine it in the present, on the border between past and future — that is, outside of time, which is impossible.

(3) No matter how much harder we make it to trace the causes, we never arrive at a conception of complete freedom, that is, of an absence of cause. However inaccessible to us the cause of any expression of will may be, whether our own or someone else's, the first demand of reason is to assume a cause and go looking for it, because no phenomenon is conceivable without one. I raise my arm to perform an action independent of any cause — but my very wish to perform an action without a cause is itself the cause of my action.

But even granting — by imagining a man wholly exempt from every influence, considering only his momentary action in the present, unprompted by any cause — that we could reduce this remaining element of inevitability to something infinitely small, equal to zero, we still would not have arrived at a conception of complete freedom in man, because a being uninfluenced by the external world, standing outside time and independent of cause, is no longer a man at all.
In the same way, we can never imagine the action of a man entirely without freedom and wholly subject to the law of inevitability.
