(1) However much we increase our knowledge of the spatial conditions in which a man is situated, that knowledge can never be complete, because the number of those conditions is as infinite as space itself. And so, as long as not every condition influencing a man has been identified, there is no complete inevitability, and a certain measure of freedom always remains.

(2) However much we lengthen the period of time between the action we are examining and our judgment of it, that period will always be finite, while time itself is infinite, and so here too there can never be absolute inevitability.
(3) However accessible the chain of causation behind any action may be, we will never know the whole of it, since it has no end — and so again we never arrive at absolute inevitability.

But beyond this, even if, granting that the remaining minimum of freedom equals zero, we assumed in some particular case — say, that of a dying man, an unborn child, or an idiot — a complete absence of freedom, by doing so we would destroy the very conception of man in the case we are examining, because the moment there is no freedom, there is also no man. And so the conception of a man's action subject solely to the law of inevitability, with no element of freedom at all, is just as impossible as the conception of a man's completely free action.

And so, to imagine the action of a man entirely subject to the law of inevitability, without any freedom, we would have to assume knowledge of an infinite number of spatial relations, an infinitely long period of time, and an infinite chain of causes.
To imagine a man perfectly free, not subject to the law of inevitability at all, we would have to imagine him utterly alone, beyond space, beyond time, and free of any dependence on cause.

In the first case, if inevitability were possible without freedom, we would have arrived at a definition of inevitability purely by the laws of inevitability itself — that is, a mere form without content.

In the second case, if freedom were possible without inevitability, we would have arrived at an unconditioned freedom beyond space, time, and cause, which, precisely because it was unconditioned and unlimited, would amount to nothing — mere content without form.
We would, in fact, have arrived at the two fundamentals out of which man's whole view of the universe is built: the incomprehensible essence of life, and the laws that define that essence.

Reason says: (1) space, along with every form of matter that makes it visible, is infinite, and cannot be imagined otherwise. (2) Time is infinite motion, without a single moment of rest, and cannot be thought of otherwise. (3) The connection between cause and effect has no beginning and can have no end.

Consciousness says: (1) I alone exist, and everything that exists is nothing but me; therefore I contain space within myself. (2) I measure the flow of time by the fixed moment of the present, the only moment in which I am conscious of myself as alive; therefore I stand outside time. (3) I am beyond cause, because I feel myself to be the cause of every manifestation of my own life.
Reason gives voice to the laws of inevitability. Consciousness gives voice to the essence of freedom.
Freedom limited by nothing is the essence of life, as it appears in man's consciousness. Inevitability without content is man's reason, in its three forms.
Freedom is the thing examined. Inevitability is what does the examining. Freedom is the content. Inevitability is the form.

Only by separating these two sources of knowledge, related to one another as form is related to content, do we arrive at the mutually exclusive, separately incomprehensible conceptions of freedom and inevitability.
Only by uniting them do we get a clear conception of man's life.
Apart from these two concepts, which in their union define one another as form and content, no conception of life is possible at all.
Everything we know about the life of man is nothing but a certain relation between free will and inevitability — that is, between consciousness and the laws of reason.
Everything we know about the external world of nature is likewise nothing but a certain relation between the forces of nature and inevitability, or between the essence of life and the laws of reason.

The great forces of nature lie outside us, and we are not conscious of them; we call those forces gravitation, inertia, electricity, animal force, and so on. But we are conscious of the force of life within man, and we call that freedom.

But just as the force of gravitation, incomprehensible in itself yet felt by every man, is only intelligible to us to the extent that we know the laws of inevitability it is subject to — from the first realization that all bodies have weight, up to Newton's law — so too the force of free will, incomprehensible in itself yet something everyone is conscious of, is only intelligible to us to the extent that we know the laws of inevitability it is subject to — from the fact that every man dies, all the way up to knowledge of the most complex economic and historical laws.
All knowledge is simply a matter of bringing this essence of life under the laws of reason.

Man's free will differs from every other force in that man is directly conscious of it, but to reason, it is no different from any other force at all. The forces of gravitation, electricity, or chemical affinity are only distinguished from one another by how reason defines them. In just the same way, the force of man's free will is distinguished by reason from the other forces of nature only by the definition reason gives it. Freedom, apart from necessity, that is, apart from the laws of reason that define it, is in no way different from gravitation, or heat, or the force that makes things grow — to reason, it is nothing but a momentary, undefinable sensation of life.

And just as the undefinable essence of the force moving the heavenly bodies, the undefinable essence of the forces of heat and electricity, or of chemical affinity, or of the vital force, forms the content of astronomy, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and so on, in exactly the same way the force of free will forms the content of history. But just as the subject of every science is the manifestation of this unknown essence of life, while that essence itself can only be the subject of metaphysics, so too the manifestation of the force of free will in human beings, in space, in time, and in dependence on cause, forms the subject of history, while free will itself is the subject of metaphysics.

In the experimental sciences, what we know we call the laws of inevitability; what we don't know we call vital force. Vital force is merely an expression for the unknown remainder left over, beyond what we know, of the essence of life.

So too in history: what is known to us we call the laws of inevitability; what is unknown we call free will. Free will, for history, is merely an expression for the unknown remainder of what we know about the laws of human life.

History examines the manifestations of man's free will in connection with the external world, in time, and in dependence on cause — that is, it defines this freedom by the laws of reason, and so history is a science only to the extent that this free will is defined by those laws.

Treating man's free will as something capable of influencing historical events — that is, as a force not subject to law — would be the same for history as the recognition of a free force moving the heavenly bodies would be for astronomy.

That assumption would destroy the very possibility of there being laws at all — of there being any science whatsoever. If even a single body moves freely, the laws of Kepler and Newton are overturned, and no conception of the movement of the heavenly bodies survives. If a single action is due to free will, then not one historical law can exist, and no conception of historical events either.

For history, there exist lines along which human wills move, lines whose one end is lost in the unknown, but at whose other end a man's conscious will, in the present, moves through space, time, and dependence on cause.
The more this field of motion opens up before our eyes, the more evident the laws governing that movement become. Discovering and defining those laws is the task of history.

From the standpoint history now occupies, on the path it currently follows — looking for the causes of events in man's free will — a scientific statement of those laws is impossible, because however restricted man's free will may be, the moment we treat it as a force not subject to law, the existence of any law becomes impossible.

Only by shrinking this element of free will down to the infinitesimal — that is, by treating it as an infinitely small quantity — can we convince ourselves of the absolute inaccessibility of the causes, and only then, instead of searching for causes, will history be able to take the discovery of laws as its task.

The search for these laws has long since begun, and the new ways of thinking that history must adopt are being worked out at the very same time as the old method of history — endlessly dissecting and re-dissecting the causes of phenomena — moves toward its own self-destruction.

Every human science has traveled this same road. On reaching the infinitesimal, mathematics, the most exact of sciences, abandons the process of analysis and takes up a new process, the integration of unknown, infinitely small quantities. Setting aside the conception of cause, mathematics looks instead for law — that is, for the property common to all these unknown, infinitely small elements.

The other sciences have proceeded, in a different form, along that same path of reasoning. When Newton stated the law of gravity, he did not say that the sun or the earth possessed a property of attraction; he said that all bodies, from the largest to the smallest, have the property of attracting one another — that is, setting aside the question of what causes the bodies to move, he expressed the property common to all of them, from the infinitely large to the infinitely small. The natural sciences do the same: setting the question of cause aside, they search for laws. History stands on that same path. And if history's real object is to study the movement of nations and of humanity, and not simply to narrate episodes from the lives of individuals, then it too, setting aside the conception of cause, should search for the laws common to all the inseparably interconnected, infinitesimal elements of free will.

From the moment Copernicus's law was discovered and proved, the simple recognition that it was not the sun but the earth that moved was enough to destroy the ancients' entire picture of the cosmos. By disproving that law, it might have been possible to hold onto the old conception of how the heavenly bodies moved; but without disproving it, it would seem impossible to keep studying the Ptolemaic universe. And yet, even after Copernicus's law was discovered, the Ptolemaic universe went on being studied for a long time.

From the moment the first person stated and proved that the number of births, or of crimes, is governed by mathematical laws, that a given form of government is determined by certain geographic and economic conditions, and that certain relations between population and land produce the migrations of peoples, the foundations on which history had been built were, in essence, destroyed.

By refuting these new laws, the old view of history might have been preserved; but without refuting them, it would seem impossible to go on studying historical events as the results of man's free will. Because if a given form of government was established, or a given migration of peoples took place, as a consequence of such and such geographic, ethnographic, or economic conditions, then the free will of the individuals who appear to us to have established that form of government, or brought about the migration, can no longer be regarded as the cause.

And yet the old kind of history continues to be studied side by side with the laws of statistics, geography, political economy, comparative philology, and geology — laws that directly contradict its own assumptions.

The struggle between the old views and the new was long and stubbornly fought out in the philosophy of the physical world. Theology stood guard over the old views and accused the new ones of violating revelation. But once the truth had won out, theology settled itself just as firmly onto the new foundation.

Just as long and just as stubborn is the struggle now underway between the old and the new conception of history, and theology, in the same way, stands guard over the old view and accuses the new one of undermining revelation.

In both cases, on both sides, the struggle stirs up passion and smothers the truth. On one side there is fear, and regret at the thought of losing the whole edifice built up over centuries; on the other, a passion for tearing it down.

To the men who fought against the emerging truths of physical philosophy, it seemed that admitting that truth would destroy faith in God, in the creation of the firmament, and in the miracle of Joshua the son of Nun. To the defenders of the laws of Copernicus and Newton — to Voltaire, for example — it seemed that the laws of astronomy destroyed religion, and he used the law of gravitation as a weapon against it.

Just so, it now seems as though the moment we admit the law of inevitability, we destroy the conception of the soul, of good and evil, and every institution of church and state built upon those conceptions.

And just so, uninvited defenders of the law of inevitability today, like Voltaire in his own time, use that law as a weapon against religion — even though the law of inevitability in history, like the law of Copernicus in astronomy, far from destroying the foundation on which the institutions of church and state are built, actually strengthens it.

Just as in the question of astronomy then, so in the question of history now, the whole disagreement rests on whether or not we accept something absolute as the measure of visible phenomena. In astronomy it was the fixity of the earth; in history it is the independence of the individual personality — free will.

Just as in astronomy the difficulty of accepting the earth's motion lay in giving up the immediate sensation of the earth's fixity and of the planets' motion, so in history the difficulty of accepting that personality is subject to the laws of space, time, and cause lies in giving up the direct feeling of one's own independence. But just as in astronomy the new view said, "It's true that we don't feel the earth moving, but by assuming it stands still we arrive at absurdity, while by assuming it moves, though we don't feel it, we arrive at laws," so too in history the new view says, "It's true that we aren't conscious of our own dependence, but by assuming we have free will we arrive at absurdity, while by assuming our dependence on the external world, on time, and on cause, we arrive at laws."

In the first case, it was necessary to give up the consciousness of an unreal fixity in space, and to accept a motion we could not feel; in the present case, it is just as necessary to give up a freedom that does not exist, and to accept a dependence we are not conscious of.
